#1289. What do various cancers have in common?

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Joanna Maria Kalucka is in the Department of Biomedicine, Aarhus University, Aarhus 8000, Denmark, and at the Steno Diabetes Center Aarhus, Aarhus University Hospital.

Cancers arising in distinct organs differ in their cellular organization, genetic alterations and patterns of how they progress1. Now, a large-scale analysis reveals striking similarities between the non-malignant cells found in the tumour microenvironment (TME) — the local environment in and around a tumour, in which non-malignant cells interact with cancer cells — across various types of cancer. Writing in Nature, Januszyk et al.2 integrate single-cell data from 42 types of tumour in humans and mice. The authors identify recurring patterns of gene activity in immune cells and in stromal cells, which contribute to tissue structure and function. These similarities provide a starting point for testing whether treatments directed at the non-cancerous cells of the TME might be effective across a range of cancer types.

#1288. Dybala ‘proud’ of Roma’s Champions League return and claims: ‘I want to end my career in Italy’

Paulo Dybala says he is proud to have helped bring Roma back to the Champions League, and hopes to finish his career in Italy.

Speaking to UEFA’s official channels, with quotes via CalcioMercato, the Argentine was speaking ahead of Roma’s league-phase trip to Paris Saint-Germain on Wednesday. Kick-off at the Parc des Princes is 21:00 CET [20:00 GMT].

The Giallorossi go into the game with four points after their defeat to Manchester United, while the holders have won all four of their matches so far.

“In my first years here, it was obviously a disappointment not to be able to bring Roma back to the Champions League. I also felt responsible,” Dybala said.

“In my first year, we came close by reaching the Europa League final, but in the years that followed we didn’t do enough to deserve it. Last year, though, I saw a truly determined team. We showed that by keeping clean sheets in the last few games, because we knew qualification didn’t depend only on us until the final matchday.

“It was a moment of great pride for me, because I could see how happy the fans were to be back in the Champions League, just like we were. We want to test ourselves against the best teams in Europe, and now we can.”

Dybala has stayed fit far more often under Gian Piero Gasperini, and he credited the coach’s approach.

“Physically, knee operations aside, I’ve felt very good over the last year, especially muscularly,” he said.

“The coach and his staff, including the fitness coaches who arrived this year, gave me a limited but appropriate workload in pre-season so I could always be available. So far this season, I’ve felt in good shape and I’m very happy.”

Dybala signed a one-year contract until 30 June 2027 in July. Now in his 15th year in Italy, after spells at Palermo and Juventus before moving to Roma in 2022, he made clear he has no intention of leaving.

“I never imagined I’d have a career like this, let alone spend 15 years in Italy. I’ve lived in the south, the north, and now the centre of the country. I’ve been here for almost half my life and I’m very happy,” he said.

“Italy welcomed me with open arms. My daughter was born here, so she’s Italian. Yes, I hope to stay in Italy for the rest of my career. It would be very special for me to dedicate an entire career to Serie A, as well as the year I spent in Serie B, which was very important for me.”

Manchester United could face a significant financial hurdle in pursuing Everton defender Jarrad Branthwaite, as the centre-back’s potential transfer valuation has now emerged.

The Red Devils have been interested in the 24-year-old for some time, but failed to secure his services in the summer of 2024. However, a fresh move could require a considerably bigger investment than their previous attempts.

According to Football Insider, former Everton scout Bryan King believes the Merseyside club could demand between £ 70 m and £ 80 m to sanction the defender’s departure.

King believes Branthwaite’s performances and Everton’s continued progress make him an attractive proposition for bigger clubs. He also highlighted the defender’s previous injury problems but suggested his recent displays should keep interest in his services strong.

The former scout also questioned Manchester United’s defensive options, suggesting the club needs far more than one new centre-back to improve their backline.

Everton are in a particularly strong negotiating position after securing Branthwaite’s future with a five-year contract in 2025. The Toffees have little reason to entertain a cut-price departure, especially given his importance to their long-term plans.

Want more CaughtOffside coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for news you can trust.

United previously had a £ 50 million offer rejected for the English defender in 2024, and their continued admiration could put Everton under pressure if another approach materialises.

Branthwaite reportedly agreed personal terms with the Old Trafford outfit then, although a transfer never came to fruition.

The defender could be an attractive addition for United, given his physical presence, Premier League experience and potential to become a long-term defensive leader.

However, spending up to £ 80 million to secure his signature would be a major investment. Whether United are prepared to meet Everton’s demands remains uncertain, but the Toffees have made their position clear through the valuation suggested by King.

#1286. Aston Villa 2.0 are making mockery of the early-season doom merchants

Two months ago there were many doom merchants insisting that Aston Villa were heading for a season of struggle, but they are looking foolish now.

After a summer of uncertainty and much change, Villa are stepping into a brave new era and find themselves joint-top of the Champions League table after three matches.

With co-owner Nassef Sawiris in attendance, Villa fans are dreaming of another magical season almost four years after Emery walked through the doors at this historic club.

Sawiris was the key figure driving Emery’s appointment in October 2022 and few could have predicted the success that has followed with the Basque manager at the helm.

Villa 2.0 have made a flawless start to their European campaign and are running into form in the Premier League after a sticky start.

In this comfortable victory over Viking, Villa became the second fastest team to win 20 matches at this level from 30 matches, only behind Real Madrid (who won 20 of their first 29). They have also won 12 home games in Europe in a row.

Much tougher assignments are to come, with powerhouses Barcelona, Paris St-Germain and Borussia Dortmund still to come in the league phase.

Yet Villa are currently level on points with Paris St-Germain, Liverpool and Real Madrid, and Emery remains determined to make an impact in this competition.

He said: “We are delighted with how we are responding and improving things. The Champions League is very difficult, but we have nine points and you can feel confidence. We are comfortable for the next challenge.”

What a difference a few months make. Over the course of the summer, many observers wondered if the Emery fairy tale was in danger of ending.

With six of the starting XI from last season’s Europa League final victory moving on, it could have been a difficult period of transition. We have all learnt, however, that Emery can never be written off or doubted.

Just a week after their biggest European win, the 6-0 destruction of Fenerbahce, expectations were understandably high. Before kick-off a huge tifo was unfurled in the Holte End with the words: “We’ve conquered before. We’re prepared for more.”

This was not as comfortable but still an impressive performance from this new and exciting team. Alysson, the Brazilian winger, was their man of the match.

Emery had warned his players of complacency against the Norwegian champions, but Villa took command from the start and were ahead after 23 minutes.

Ross Barkley scored twice against Fenerbahce last week and was in the right place again to head Ibrahim Mbaye’s corner past Arild Ostbo.

#1285. The two things Roberto De Zerbi demanded from Luca Williams-Barnett's first Tottenham start as 18-year-old star signs new lucrative deal, writes MATT BARLOW

Published: 08:08 EST, 22 November 2026 | Updated: 18:17 EST, 24 November 2026

Having summoned Luca Williams-Barnett to his office to let the teenager know he would be making his first Premier League start, Roberto De Zerbi could not resist a little bit of fun.

De Zerbi cast a serious demeanour and told him he had weighed the options and figured the best course of action would be 60 minutes with the Under-21s.

Williams-Barnett did not hide his disappointment. 'Why, do you think you are ready to start for the first team?' asked the Spurs boss. The 18-year-old said he thought so.

De Zerbi cracked a smile and told him he was in the team against Ipswich but demanded two things in return.

First, that his young star would play with freedom as though 'in the park with friends' and second that he would work without the ball in the manner of the world's best players in his position, such as Lamine Yamal.

This is where the comparisons to Yamal emerged soon after Williams-Barnett lit up the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium. On Tuesday, he was rewarded for his progress with a new contract at the club.

He said: 'This is a special moment for me and my family, and one I have worked really hard to reach. But this is only the start.

Luca Williams-Barnett scored his first Premier League goal for Tottenham on his first start in the top flight

The talented academy youngster may not be lightning fast but he has pace and creates goals

'Spurs is a family to me. I've been here for so long – it's a second home, where I trust the people and coaches who have pushed me to become the player I am today.

'The club has trusted and believed in me, now I'm ready to repay that.'

Hopes are indeed high. Similarities with Yamal are evident in physique, his fluency of movement on the ball and the bursts of pace, the way they look to play. Even the hairstyle.

Just as Yamal, a left footer, likes to operate wide on the right for Barcelona and Spain, De Zerbi deployed Williams-Barnett as a right footer on the left, although most of his youth career has been spent centrally in the No 10 position.

He does not possess what you would consider in modern football to be exceptional pace, but he is quick, and his strengths are on the ball. He likes the ball. He creates. And he scores goals.

From wide on the left against Ipswich, he scored within 15 minutes, darting in at the back post to finish, and created the second for Dominic Solanke, with a 60-yard run from inside his own half and cross with his left foot.

His brilliance lit up the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium, where there has not been a lot to celebrate in the last 18 months. Terrible home form was the crux of last season's relegation fears.

Here, they rose to salute a new talent, one of their own. One De Zerbi believes has the attitude to match his outrageous talent. Confident, certainly. Aware of his natural gifts and his technical skills. Perhaps bordering on arrogance when on the pitch.

De Zerbi was pleased to see Williams-Barnett, in a seat nearby on the team bus from the training ground to the stadium, watching YouTube clips of Ronaldinho, Eden Hazard and Neymar.

The Spurs boss, who has faith in the power of inspirational video footage, took this as a positive sign. The youngster was relaxed but more than this he had a passion for football and always looking to learn.

'I'm positive about his character and behaviour because I've been working with him for three or four months and I know him enough,' said De Zerbi, whose tactical instructions involved James Maddison operating closely to Williams-Barnett, a kindred spirit in a footballing sense able to talk him through the game.

When the teenager set off on the swaggering run for Solanke's goal, Maddison could be seen nearby urging him forward into the ocean of space left open by Ipswich.

The 18-year-old had rival clubs circling but Spurs have now tied him down

Born and raised in Luton, Williams-Barnett comes from a strong, grounded family - which will only help as he looks to assimilate into the senior side

Spurs have prioritised Premier League experience in the transfer market under De Zerbi to create a more mature dressing room environment. Signings such as Andy Robertson have been key to this.

The policy is not purely for the benefit of academy graduates stepping into the first-team environment, but it does help when it comes to setting the standards required in elite sport.

Anyone gifted enough to break into the Spurs squad will have been feted as a star through the youth development phase and well rewarded to resist others trying to lure them away.

Williams-Barnett was under contract until 2028 but his new deal means clubs circling must now look elsewhere.

It is easy for impressionable teens to become conceited in this situation. Williams-Barnett has had discipline and time-keeping issues but most at Spurs speak of a young man devoted to his football from a strong, loving family who are sure to keep him grounded.

He was born and raised in Luton, starting out in Luton Town's pre-academy to Under 10s, before Spurs paid a small fee for him.

His father Jonathan Barnett was a central midfielder in Step Three of non-league football, known as 'Jono' and playing for various clubs in the region including Dunstable Town and Arlesey Town and renowned for his passing, set pieces and with an eye for goal.

Although more of a dribbler, Luca grew up with football in the family, polishing his technical skills with his dad in the back garden. 'He is from a very good family and it's crucial for this type of players,' said De Zerbi.

Spurs have been here before, of course, with talented teens breaking through with N17 at their feet.

There was Mikey Moore's wonderful cameo against AZ Alkmaar after which Ange Postecoglou called for patience and commonsense, and Maddison went on TV and said it was 'like having Neymar on the left wing'.

There was Jose Mourinho taking the match ball from Son Heung-min, who had just scored the most incredible solo goal against Burnley, and handing it to Troy Parrott on his Premier League debut.

There was Mauricio Pochettino dubbing Marcus Edwards his 'mini Messi'. Pochettino soon came to wish he had not burdened Edwards with such lavish praise.

The pitfalls are well known and progress is rarely a smooth upward trajectory. It is a balancing act between maximising potential and getting carried away.

De Zerbi is quietly confident Williams-Barnett has what it takes to handle the hype.

On the new deal, thought to be for five years, the manager said: 'Luca is a player I think the world of, and I'm so happy that he has signed a new contract.

'He has benefitted from being around the first team every day, growing in stature and consistency, and has deserved his place in the matchday squad over recent weeks.

'Everyone can see how technically gifted Luca is on the pitch but I also love his calmness and decision-making under pressure.

'The best players have confidence on the pitch and humility off it. There is still plenty of room for Luca to improve, and I know he will continue to work hard every day to be the best version of himself.'

#1282. AI is ditching hallucinated references — and other bad habits

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Hallucinated academic citations have become a hallmark of the artificial-intelligence era. But they might soon be gone for good. Researchers have found that the latest large language models (LLMs) rarely, if ever, attribute information to sources that don’t exist.

The finding is part of an analysis that reports that many LLM tendencies, such as overthinking simple mathematics problems and complying with illogical requests, fade over time as AI companies release new or updated models with improved capabilities. Many of these tendencies disappear about 16 months after the phenomenon is first described in a published paper. The analysis, described in a blogpost, has not been peer reviewed.

“We, as users of these systems, need to not have such a fixed view of what AI can do and what it can’t do,” says co-author Owen Queen, an AI researcher at Stanford University in California.

But just because an LLM behaviour fades as models improve doesn’t mean that the effect immediately disappears, says Maxim Topaz, a health-care AI researcher at Columbia University in New York City. Topaz has found1 that the number of hallucinated citations in academic papers has risen drastically since 2023, probably because more researchers than ever before are using LLMs, and they often aren’t using the latest models.

Queen and his colleague identified 50 widely cited LLM behaviours that were described in publications between late 2022, when some of the first LLMs became widely available, and late 2025. They then gave the same prompts that first elicited the behaviour in the original publications to 20 LLMs that were released from mid-2024 to late 2026 to see if the effect has strengthened or weakened over time. For example, they asked each model to count the number of r’s in ‘strawberry’ — something that LLMs have found difficult but can now do more reliably.

Nearly half of the behaviours they checked have largely disappeared from newer models, leading the researchers to deem those effects ‘expired’. Expired behaviours had an average lifespan of about 16 months after publication, although some were fleeting — models stopped overthinking simple maths problems just a month and a half after this tendency was published. Other traits persisted, such as the stereotyping of Black women by disproportionately describing them as resilient, which lasted for longer than three years.

Although most of the retested LLM behaviours have faded over time, three have become more pronounced. Today’s models praise what their users like even more often than they used to, LLMs favour their own writing more strongly than that of other LLMs and people; and LLMs are now even worse than they used to be at generating truly random numbers.

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03753-1

Article  PubMed  Google Scholar

Bruno Fernandes has put discussions over a new Manchester United contract on hold, insisting the club’s immediate priority should be winning football matches rather than deciding his future.

The United captain’s situation has attracted considerable attention after two contract proposals were reportedly rejected, but his latest comments provide important context.

Fernandes is not suggesting his Old Trafford career is over. Instead, he believes negotiations should wait while Mauricio Pochettino attempts to drag United away from the wrong end of the Premier League table.

As reported by Fabrizio Romano, Fernandes has confirmed that contract discussions have stopped for the time being.

“Contract talks have stopped for us to start winning games… and then we can talk about contract”.

“It’s not important now. It’s my future, I haven’t got much left in my contract, but we will have time to speak about that”.

United are not completely exposed despite the uncertainty. Fernandes’ existing agreement expires next summer, but the club hold an option to extend it until 2028.

A CaughtOffside report also highlights that United have offered their captain a new contract, while Fernandes has dismissed suggestions that his stance is motivated by demands for more money or additional years.

This feels less like Fernandes rejecting Man United and more like the captain challenging the club to give him a reason to commit.

At 32, his next contract could determine where he spends the final years of his career at the highest level. Signing another long-term agreement while United are struggling near the bottom of the table would require enormous faith in the latest rebuild.

Pochettino therefore has an important role.

Improved results, smart January recruitment and evidence of a clear footballing direction could do more to convince Fernandes than simply increasing his salary.

United should activate their extension if necessary, protecting themselves from losing such a valuable player cheaply.

But the long-term solution is not contractual leverage. It is proving to Fernandes that Old Trafford remains the right place to compete for major trophies.

His message is ultimately straightforward: fix the football first, and discuss the future afterwards.

#1280. THE END GAME? Writing is on the wall for McCann after revitalised Dons ran riot at Rugby Park

Published: 18:00 EST, 22 November 2026 | Updated: 18:11 EST, 22 November 2026

Let’s face it, Neil McCann was never the most popular of appointments with Kilmarnock fans, but not even his harshest critics could deny that he did a fine job in keeping the club in Scotland’s top flight last season.

Unfortunately for him, it looks increasingly likely that he isn’t going to get the chance to repeat the trick this time around.

The writing already appears to be on the wall for the 52-year-old. A question of when, rather than if, he is given his jotters.

By all accounts, he hasn’t lost the dressing room. Which is just as well, because he has well and truly lost the punters, whose collective mood shifted from angry to apathetic over the course of 90-odd thoroughly entertaining minutes at Rugby Park on Saturday.

McCann knows this himself. It is not as if he is operating with the blinkers on.

It's a tough watch for Neil McCann as his Kilmarnock team go down 4-2 to Aberdeen

His assessment of his team’s performances week-to-week tends to be pretty honest, as it was again this weekend.

The problem is, as he put it, that he is coming across ‘like a broken record’.

His team are hopeless at the back and toothless up top, with some encouraging stuff in between. If the supporters are sick of hearing it, imagine how scunnered McCann must feel saying it. He certainly looks it.

If they continue to defend like this, relegation is a nailed-on certainty.

They shipped four here — and it could have very easily been a few more — to take their tally to 33 conceded for the season in just 14 games. It’s laughable, there’s no other way to dress it up.

Aberdeen’s Kevin Nisbet scored twice in four first-half minutes, capitalising on a woeful clearance from keeper Nico Mantl to put the Dons ahead, before curling a free-kick straight through the weakest wall you’ve ever seen in your life to double the visitors’ advantage.

New Dons boss Mario Frick can't hide his delight after victory in first game in charge

The third goal — shortly after Greg Kiltie had given McCann’s men a lifeline — was the worst of the lot. Former Rugby Park skipper Brad Lyons ghosted in behind the completely unaware Michael Schjonning-Larsen to head the ball home after Cathal McCarthy failed to stop Nesta Guinness-Walker’s cross from the left touchline.

Shocking stuff all round, and exactly the type of goal which has killed Killie all season — and will continue to do so until something drastic changes.

Let’s not forget, the recent international break afforded McCann and his staff a fortnight to work on things on the training pitch ahead of what is going to be a gruelling winter schedule.

While the Killie manager will ultimately be the one to pay the price, his players need to have a right good look at themselves too. There was simply no sign of anyone in that backline taking any sort of responsibility.

Kilmarnock’s next three games are against St Mirren, Hibernian and Motherwell — the three sides currently directly above them in the table.

An absolute minimum of four points from that run is required, otherwise this is going to get rather ugly. In truth, defeat in Paisley this weekend may well be the final nail in McCann’s coffin.

On the other hand, things are finally starting to look up for the Dons.

New manager Mario Frick has promised to bring heavy metal football to these shores, and if Saturday is anything to go by, the ex-Liechtenstein international is a man of his word.

McCann's job looks to be on the line after bottom club Killie succumbed to another defeat

His team were a joy to watch going forward here, particularly in the first half.

It was a million miles away from the kind of turgid football offered up under his predecessor as Dons manager, Stephen Robinson.

Speed, intensity, aggression, quality. The performance was full of it.

You could count the number of times the Dons faffed about with the ball on one hand. Every time there was an opportunity to get forward, they took it.

Ante Palaversa, making his first appearance of the campaign, was at the heart of it.

For whatever reason, Robinson never fancied the Croatian, a stance which perplexed the Pittodrie faithful. Indeed, the 26-year-old — once on the books of Manchester City — was deemed surplus to requirements over the summer.

The Dons will be delighted there were no takers.

He was outstanding here as he commanded that space between midfield and defence without breaking sweat. Nobody in Killie colours could get near him.

Both Nicky Devlin and Guinness-Walker bombed up their respective wings all day, while some of the link-up play between Nisbet — who should have had a hat-trick before Findlay Marshall wrapped things up late on — and Hicham Mahou was delightful.

Defensively, they were all over the shop at times, and no doubt they will be punished heavily at Ibrox on Tuesday night if they are as open as this.

But this was a display to simply be enjoyed rather than picked apart. It makes a change.

#1279. Harry Kane proves there is only one Ballon d’Or winner

Let’s cut to the chase. If there is any justice, sanity or logic in football then Harry Kane will win the Ballon d’Or when the ceremony takes place in London on Monday.

Arsenal would have deservedly won this Champions League match away to Bayern Munich if Kane was not on the pitch. Instead, they almost lost it but for another bit of brilliance from Declan Rice, Kane’s vice-captain for England, and probably his successor to wear the armband.

“I’m lucky I can play with him and not so lucky I have to play against him,” Rice said, and that summed it up succinctly.

And that Ballon d’Or? There is bias, but Rice – who is also on the 30-strong list of nominees – added of Kane: “He is the clear winner. His numbers speak for themselves, the year he has had has been remarkable. When you play with him you realise how good he is and when you play against him you see how much of a pain it is.”

Arsenal stood toe-to-toe with Bayern in an open match. Both sides went for it, partly because they knew under the Champions League format, that defeat was not a disaster. There has been some chat about whether Arsenal can be, well, a bit dull. Not here. It would be no surprise to see these two face off again deep into this competition.

The only setback for Arsenal was a worrying injury to Bukayo Saka early on, limping off and tapping his thigh, indicating an issue with his muscle. Mikel Arteta’s reaction betrayed his understandable concern.

Kane won a penalty and then expertly took it to give Bayern the lead. Other strikers could have scored the penalty but few would have created the wonderful assist that drew Bayern level.

It has been a fact for quite some years that Kane is not only the best goalscorer for England but the best passer. Indeed, if Kane could provide for Kane he would have scored even more goals.

“Unsere nummer neun,” shouted the stadium announcer after Kane’s goal and that needed no translation. Kane is a god in Bavaria, where they know a few things about having great centre-forwards. But the 33-year-old is surpassing them all.

Kane’s goal meant he had scored in 10 straight Champions League games, one short of the record held by Cristiano Ronaldo. It was also the former Tottenham Hotspur forward’s 16th goal in 23 games against Arsenal. No one has ever scored more against them.

Kane is the complete player, carrying out his defensive duties – winning headers to clear Bayern’s lines from Arsenal free-kicks – to linking the play to being the focus of his team’s attacks. He is a centre-half, central midfielder and centre-forward. Who pops up on the wing to deliver pinpoint crosses.

Maybe Kane will be pipped at the Palladium – the theatre where the ceremony takes place – by Barcelona’s Lamine Yamal or Real Madrid’s Kylian Mbappé, or even an absurd sympathy vote for Lionel Messi. But Kane deserves it. His time is now.

Some passages of play in the first half deserve analysis. Just to highlight how good Kane was. After an Arsenal corner, wastefully volleyed over by Riccardo Calafiori, Bayern countered and suddenly it was three on two. Serge Gnabry, the former Arsenal winger, had to do better than shoot weakly when picked out on the overlap. David Raya saved. That was a let-off.

But who sprung that counter? It was not Manuel Neuer, the Bayern goalkeeper, taking the goal-kick, but Kane, with his sharp thinking. And then Kane launched a superb pass from deep which Ismael Saibari should have dealt with better. It should have been another opportunity. Potentially a goal.

This should all work in Arsenal’s favour, and Mikel Arteta will be looking for a repeat of the energy and quality that his team showed against Bayern last season. Some excellent, if disquieting, detail from Sam Dean in this piece about the mood around Arsenal away from the first-team following the news of 60 planned redundancies. Sam writes that there are expecting to be other experienced and influential figures departing. The timing of cuts invites particular scrutiny, coming after the emotional peak of winning the league, record revenues and Mikel Arteta’s new contract.

After Arsenal were beaten by Bayern Munich in a Champions League quarter-final two years ago, Mikel Arteta bemoaned a lack of “magic moments” in attack.

Arsenal have since progressed to a Champions League semi-final and final, while ending a 22-year wait for a Premier League title.

The upward trajectory has translated to tangible success, but Arsenal are still searching the level-raising attacker they lacked on their last visit to the Allianz Arena in 2024.

Back then, Arsenal’s offensive game revolved around Kai Havertz, Bukayo Saka and Martin Odegaard and that remains the case, which makes one wonder if Arsenal’s forward options have been adequately renewed.

A pair of stodgy performances (in victory) against Leeds United and Nottingham Forest have amplified those questions, though some of Arsenal’s slicker football in the season’s early weeks has been forgotten a little hastily.

They have made another strong start to another European campaign with six points from six, but this is undoubtedly their hardest fixture of the league phase.

Their chances of matching last season’s eight wins from eight could well hinge on the outcome of tonight’s game, but there are worse times to face Bayern.

Vincent Kompany’s team looks as formidable as ever, having scored 22 goals from six Bundesliga games so far this season. Their rotational approach is hard to track, with runners from deep breaking beyond Harry Kane who wanders into deep midfield positions.

However, they are without Michael Olise (suspension) and Jamal Musiala (injury) while Joshua Kimmich will miss the game on compassionate grounds following the death of his father.

With the exception of William Saliba, Christos Tzolis and Piero Hincacpie, Arsenal have a pretty clean bill of health and the strength of their bench was crucial against Leeds, Lille and Forest last week.

For Arteta, there are some interesting selection calls to make. It is anticipated that Jurrien Timber will replace Ben White at right-back, and first-choice left-back Riccardo Calafiori has been rested for the Champions League games so far. Should Arteta continue that policy, Myles Lewis-Skelly will fill the position, which will likely mean a midfield start for Bruno Guimarães or Mikel Merino.

Arsenal’s manager must also decide between Noni Madueke and Eberechi Eze on the left, and Viktor Gyokeres and Kai Havertz up front. Havertz is Arteta’s preference, but he also has to consider a relatively short turnaround before Saturday’s league game against Everton.

#1277. Liverpool's win over Man United was a landmark day for Andoni Iraola - he is playing a style of football that Jurgen Klopp would be proud of, writes LEWIS STEELE

Published: 02:00 EST, 23 November 2026 | Updated: 05:29 EST, 23 November 2026

A Liverpool manager wearing a toothy grin and black puffer jacket as he lapped up the adulation of Anfield with three fist bumps in front of the Kop… where have we seen that before?

Andoni Iraola may not look as natural at the grand gestures or possess the aura of his predecessor Jurgen Klopp just yet – but this still felt like a landmark day for the Basque manager.

Playing a heavy-metal style of football that Klopp would be proud of, Iraola has impressed in his early months at Liverpool but craved a real scalp against a rival to turbocharge the feeling among the fanbase and give his tenure true lift-off.

This was the finest day of the fledgling new era as Iraola’s relentless Reds were unstoppable and humiliated their biggest rivals – and the boss must be rubbing his hands at his depth of attacking weapons.

Rio Ngumoha, unbelievably still just 18, was the pick of the bunch and United simply could not get near him, while Florian Wirtz put in his best performance in a Reds shirt and Dominik Szoboszlai looked back to his breathtaking best.

Szoboszlai started the rout with a devastating free-kick and swung an imaginary golf club in celebration, then pretended to watch his tee shot fly into the Anfield Road Stand.

Andoni Iraola is playign a style of football that Jurgen Klopp would be proud of at Liverpool

Sticking on the Hungarian’s theme, the gulf in quality between these two teams felt like that of a professional golfer compared to a rookie who can barely get the ball off the driving range.

Szoboszlai got his driver out to score a thumping strike and continue his role as the Premier League’s best dead-ball specialist – and Liverpool never looked back from there.

All the talk centred around Mauricio Pochettino’s soft side and the embarrassing sequence of events that led to Lenny Yoro’s early red card but let’s take nothing away from Liverpool, who were breathtaking and unstoppable.

The fact the score was only 4-0 flattered United. To be picky and find criticism in feedback of Liverpool, they were wasteful. This could have been five, six, seven, you name it.

Ngumoha was unplayable. The England international was only four when United won the last of their league titles and Sir Alex Ferguson departed, so he will not remember this team being competent. But the teenager knew the significance of his performance in this fixture.

His assist for Florian Wirtz was eye-catching, his goal to make it 3-0 deserved after a lung-busting run off the ball. Poor Diogo Dalot will have nightmares for days about Ngumoha’s dancing feet as the Liverpool winger skipped past him time and again.

There were times when Ngumoha played the wrong pass which is the most frightening thing for rivals. This kid is far from the finished product. He will only get better and can be one of the best forwards in the game in a year or so.

He is level-headed unlike some other egotistical young stars and he plays with a smile on his face. Why wouldn’t he?

Rio Ngumoha was unplayable against Manchester United at Anfield and will only get better

Liverpool will pay a maximum of £6.8million for him, based on add-ons after poaching him from Chelsea two years ago. In the week of Grand Theft Auto IV’s release, the heist of Ngumoha feels like the grandest theft of all (though he is only just old enough to play the video game!).

Those around him are all £100million signings but his ceiling is just as high as that of Wirtz, Alexander Isak and Bradley Barcola.

It helps that all four clicked in this game. Wirtz has been excellent this season but has not performed in the bigger fixtures. Conversations after losses to Manchester City and Arsenal centred around Wirtz not showing up.

The German was everywhere here and United were left to chase shadows. It is not an exaggeration to label this his best Liverpool performance, with an easy-on-the-eye goal and some moments of creative genius.

Barcola destroyed United with his pace, Szoboszlai was a constant menace, while Isak did everything right until it came to finishing several attacks.

And that is the thing that will excite the head coach and should leave rival fans quaking in their boots. This team is full of virtuoso match-winners but all of them have plenty of room to improve. If they do that and all fulfil their potential, the sky is the limit for Iraola’s Liverpool.

Manchester United have reportedly made Bournemouth left-back Adrien Truffert their “dream target” for the January transfer window as Mauricio Pochettino looks to strengthen a struggling squad.

United’s disastrous start to the season has increased the urgency around their winter plans.

Sitting 19th in the Premier League following a 4-0 defeat to Liverpool in Pochettino’s first match in charge, the Red Devils desperately need reinforcements capable of making an immediate difference.

Truffert now appears to have moved right to the top of their defensive shopping list.

According to GIVEMESPORT, ManUnited have identified Truffert as their “dream target” for January.

The France international has been linked with United for several months, but the latest report suggests their interest has become significantly more serious following Pochettino’s arrival.

United had previously considered Newcastle United’s Lewis Hall as a leading option at left-back. However, Newcastle are determined to resist January interest in the England international, potentially making Truffert the more realistic target.

Bournemouth will not make negotiations easy either. A FootballTransfers report claimed the Cherries value Truffert at around £60million and would prefer not to sell him midway through the season.

There is plenty to like about this potential signing.

Truffert is Premier League proven, athletic and comfortable contributing at both ends of the pitch.

At 25, he is also entering his prime rather than arriving as another expensive prospect who needs several seasons to develop.

United clearly need greater reliability at left-back, particularly given Luke Shaw’s recurring fitness problems. The concern is the price.

Spending around £60m on a full-back in January would consume a significant portion of United’s available budget when Pochettino also needs improvements elsewhere.

However, their league position changes the calculation. United cannot afford to treat January as a window simply for long-term planning.

If Pochettino believes Truffert can immediately improve the defence and become his long-term first-choice left-back, United should seriously explore the deal.

The challenge will be convincing Bournemouth to sell one of their most important players halfway through a difficult season without paying an enormous January premium.

#1275. Taylor shuts down Lazio exit amid Newcastle and Juventus links: ‘I want to help the club return to the Champions League’

Kenneth Taylor has ruled out leaving Lazio in January, insisting he wants to help Gennaro Gattuso’s side return to the Champions League.

According to Il Messaggero, via TuttoMercatoWeb, the Dutch midfielder knows about the interest from Juventus and the Premier League, but has made it clear he isn’t going anywhere.

“It’s all true, my agents have informed me. But I’ve already said I’m not even thinking about leaving in January,” Taylor said. “I want to stay here and help Lazio return to the Champions League.”

The 24-year-old has become one of Serie A’s standout midfielders this season. Tuttosport reported last week that Newcastle have set their sights on him, with Bournemouth and Brentford also after the Dutchman, while Juventus are monitoring his situation.

Lazio have no intention of selling. According to the report, even €40 million might not be enough to convince Claudio Lotito and sporting director Angelo Fabiani to negotiate next summer.

Taylor’s contract already runs until 2030, but he earns only around €1.5m a season, so the club are considering a pay rise to reward his form.

It’s quite a turnaround. Taylor arrived from Ajax in January, and in July Gattuso sent him off the training pitch after a row in pre-season, leaving his future in real doubt. Instead, he has become a key part of Gattuso’s midfield as Lazio sit top of Serie A on 32 points.

He was outstanding again in Saturday’s 3-0 win over Lecce, producing a back-heel that drew comparisons with Rui Costa and completing a record 23 progressive passes.

#1274. Sore throat? The brain has surprising control over how ill you feel

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Max Kozlov is a senior reporter with Nature in Washington DC.

Researchers are beginning to show how neurons in the brain detect an infection and tailor physiological responses to fight it.Credit: Dr. Chris Henstridge/SPL

A viral cold or bacterial infection can leave you feeling miserable, but each infection produces its own mix of symptoms. Now, neuroscientists are discovering that the brain is the conductor of these responses — decoding the type of pathogen that has invaded, accessing memories of past bouts of illness and even mobilizing immune defences at the sight of a sick person.

The findings, many of which are unpublished, were presented on 15 November at the Society for Neuroscience annual meeting in Washington DC, and challenge the established view of what it means to feel unwell. Neuroscientists have long viewed neurological responses to infection as a one-size-fits-all response to inflammation, rather than a strategy tailored to the threat.

“Sickness is actually not a fixed program, although we often talk about it this way,” said Jessica Osterhout, a neurobiologist at the University of Utah in Salt Lake City, who chaired the session.

A bacterial infection and a cold caused by a virus can both result in fever and exhaustion, yet they rarely trigger the same constellation of symptoms. Bacterial infections, for instance, tend to suppress appetite much more sharply than do colds, which made Osterhout and her colleagues wonder how the brain tells various pathogens apart.

Your brain could be controlling how sick you get — and how you recover

Your brain could be controlling how sick you get — and how you recover

In unpublished experiments, Osterhout’s team compared mice injected with a bacterial toxin with those given a compound that mimics a viral infection. To see how the brain distinguished between pathogens, the researchers profiled individual cells in circumventricular organs, which are specialized structures with unusually permeable blood vessels that surround brain ventricles.

When the body has an infection, cells in the circumventricular organs switch on sets of immune-related genes and release distinct mixes of chemical signals. Those signals diffuse to nearby neurons and create distinct patterns of activity for different pathogens, allowing the brain to customize its symptom profile depending on the threat.

Rather than acting as conduits that let inflammatory signals pass unchecked from the blood into the wider brain, these structures “may actually interpret them”, Osterhout said.

Sometimes, the brain doesn’t even wait for pathogens to enter the body to rally the immune system1. Andrea Serino, a neuroscientist at Lausanne University Hospital in Switzerland, studies how the brain maps peripersonal space, which is the area around the body roughly in arm’s reach.

When Serino’s team placed volunteers in virtual reality, they found that threat-monitoring brain regions became active when avatars bearing skin lesions caused by viral or bacterial infections approached, even when the figures were beyond arm’s reach. Just 15 minutes of virtual exposure triggered a surge in frontline immune ‘sentinel’ cells in participants’ blood comparable to that induced by an influenza vaccine. This reaction did not occur when participants saw healthy-looking avatars or ones expressing fear.

These experiments suggest that the immune system uses “the predictive ability of the brain to react before pathogens enter the body”, Serino said.

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03774-w

Trabanelli, S. et al. Nature Neurosci. 28, 1968–1977 (2025).

#1273. Why Andoni Iraola - NOT Jurgen Klopp - deserves credit for fixing Florian Wirtz, Omar Berrada's Sky appearance has made things worse for Man United and is Cole Palmer at the wrong club? IAN LADYMAN on MY FOOTBALL WEEKEND

Published: 07:00 EST, 23 November 2026 | Updated: 09:00 EST, 23 November 2026

In what transpired to be a lively Sky TV studio at Anfield, Daniel Sturridge turned in one of his own performances of the season.

The former Chelsea and Liverpool striker is proving himself a pundit of real substance and he cut to the heart of one of the more ridiculous notions of the week, namely that a week away with Jurgen Klopp had solved all Florian Wirtz’s problems at a stroke.

‘I think we should give credit to Andoni Iraola,’ he said as we all breathed a sigh at the sound of some common sense.

The obsession with Klopp among many people who support and follow Liverpool remains terrifyingly real and the former Anfield manager plays to it.

But to suggest – as many who should know better have done – that Klopp managed to fix Wirtz in four sessions last week is as lazy and ridiculous as it is utterly disrespectful to current Liverpool manager Iraola.

Wirtz had a good couple of games with his national team, for sure. He scored three goals which will have done much for confidence. He was fabulous against Manchester United's ten men.

Florian Wirtz has found his form at just the right time for Liverpool

Reds boss Andoni Iraola deserves credit for the German's transformation this season

But anybody who has watched even a small portion of Liverpool’s game this season will have seen a player gradually growing in stature and finally, it seems, adjusting to the largely unique rhythms of the Premier League.

Iraola is a talented coach. Talk to players and staff at Bournemouth and they will tell you that. He improves footballers and steadily he is bringing his influence to bear on Wirtz.

The 23-year-old still has some way to go. He can still look half a yard too slow on occasion. But he has created 29 Liverpool chances from open play this season.

It tends to be the execs rather than the managers who get the blame at United but Mauricio Pochettino sadly had his fingerprints on what happened on Merseyside.

He was right to complain about the sending off of Leny Yoro. Alexander Isak was never getting the ball and referee Sam Barrott should have given himself time to consider that before getting the red card out.

In those situations the defender should be given the benefit of any doubt.

The decision has an enormous impact on the game, something that seemed to pass many people by.

Nevertheless the passage of play had at its inception a horror moment from Matthijs de Ligt that most of us could have seen coming the moment the team sheet dropped.

Sometimes it doesn’t pay for a manager to try and be the smartest bloke in the room.

Mauricio Pochettino should shoulder some of the blame for United's dismal defeat at Anfield

BERRADA INTERVENTION NOT USEFUL FOR UNITED

No doubt the decision to plonk Omar Berrada in front of a TV camera was driven by good intentions by United.

The club’s executives had been accused of hiding while Old Trafford burned so here was one of them, sitting smartly in front of a huge club crest, ready to tell the world that everything would be OK.

The only problem is that the words of Berrada, United’s chief executive, have arguably made things worse.

Berrada didn’t catch much of a break over the weekend.

Just 48 hours after telling the world that United were happy with their ‘nine defenders’  Pochettino’s team were given such a chasing at Anfield that one wondered if the new manager may be tempted to chuck all of them on at the same time.

None of this is about luck, however. Neither good nor bad. It’s about planning and the lack thereof.

Liverpool, remember, also had a big defensive problem over the summer.

Omar Berrada's surprise appearance on Sky Sports has made things worse for Man United

The two full-backs bought in the summer of 2025 – Jeremie Frimpong and Milos Kerkez – had struggled while another – Conor Bradley – was injured. In the centre, Ibrahima Konate had left for Real Madrid while young prospect Giovanni Leoni had not played since suffering a dreadful knee injury on his debut last year.

That left Virgil Van Dijk, Jeremy Jacquet and Joe Gomez. Liverpool could have struggled on. They could have counted numbers and hoped. They could have prayed for better form and fitness from the defenders they had.

But that would have been unfair on incoming manager Iraola. So in mid-August they took the Uruguayan international Ronald Araujo on loan from Barcelona and it has transpired to be a signing utterly fundamental to Liverpool’s season so far.

There was little fuss and fanfare about the deal. All the noise was reserved for the £125million winger Bradley Barcola.

But Araujo – signed as a centre-half – is a former Barcelona captain and has solved Liverpool’s right-back problem at a stroke. He was as unfussy and effective against United yesterday as he has been all season.

This is how recruitment at big clubs works. They identify problems and use their data, imagination and contacts to solve them. They don’t count the number of bodies in the dressing room and then sit on their hands telling themselves it is enough.

Every United supporter in the land could have told Berrada and his friends that United needed defensive quality in the summer. But United thought they knew best and were wrong.

It is genuinely terrifying to think just what they may do next.

The second most productive footballer in terms of assists in the league is Brighton’s Pascal Gross but the German was left as bemused as anyone as his team somehow managed to lose a game they dominated at Hull.

Brighton manager Fabian Hurzeler has said he wants his players to behave like a big team but perhaps some naivety let them down as Hull scored two in added time on Humberside.

The first of Ollie McBurnie’s goals came in the 92nd minute on the back of a quick counter and it was one that could have been stopped at source by what Pep Guardiola used to call a ‘technical foul’ – a trip or a nudge – before the ball had even crossed the halfway line.

Nobody wishes to encourage foul play but the truth is that Guardiola’s City would not have conceded that goal. Nor, for that matter, would Arsenal.

Brighton's naivety saw them suffer a surprise defeat by Hull City on Sunday

At the Etihad, Enzo Maresca gave Phil Foden a start ahead of Rayan Cherki and the City playmaker showed some glimpses of his fabulous talent.

Nevertheless the longer this period of uncertainty goes on for Foden, the harder it is to work out how it ends.

Maresca wants to play with two out and out wide players at City.

Jeremy Doku and Iliman Ndiaye started in the draw against Fulham while Antoine Semenyo will play when he is fit.

So with Cherki established as City’s creative hub just behind Haaland, Foden is on the fringes a little.

He signed a contract in June and is now tied to the club until 2030. Equally, Foden will be 27 next May and should be approaching his physical and creative peak.

Meanwhile Cole Palmer’s frustrations with life at Chelsea – highlighted in this column earlier this season – have now boiled over with a show of petulance at the end of his team’s Stamford Bridge hammering at the hands of Leeds.

The more this unfolds, the more it feels like Palmer is at the wrong club.

Palmer – for all that he tries to suggest otherwise – is an emotionally complex young athlete. He can be unpredictable and dramatic.

He needs calm around him, not persistent drift.

Cole Palmer's petulance at Stamford Bridge on Saturday has left us asking: Is he at the wrong club?

Another stunning result for Daniel Farke’s Leeds who now sit sixth in the table with the second best defensive record in the top flight.

Farke remains out of contract next summer and that still feels odd.

The club’s favourite media outlets told us last month that an ‘agreement had been reached in principle’ but still no white smoke from Elland Road.

Tottenham have crept into the top half for the first time this season after beating Ipswich with credit due to manager Roberto de Zerbi for handing teenager Luca Williams-Barnett his chance.

With big money summer signings Savio and Omar Marmoush sitting on the bench, Williams-Barnett scored the opening goal and became the fourth youngest player in history to score on his first Premier League start.

Of the three ahead of him in the list, Canadian Daniel Jebbison, now 23, currently sits on the Bournemouth bench, Danny Cadamarteri’s career became rather itinerant once he made the last of his 94 Everton league starts while Mark Cullen travelled from Hull to Bamber Bridge via outposts such as Luton, Blackpool, Port Vale, Hartlepool and Fylde.

Williams-Barnett will have enjoyed his weekend but history tells us the road ahead may not be straight.

Luca Williams-Barnett became the fourth youngest debut goalscorer in Premier League history

Of the new managers in this season’s top division, it has taken time for some to find their feet.

Iraola now has a statement Anfield win, for example, while at Bournemouth and Fulham Marco Rose and Alvaro Arbeloa no longer have to look at the league table through their fingers.

At Newcastle, it appears rather more complicated.

Eddie Howe’s replacement Matthias Jaissle doesn’t look chuffed with the players he was handed in the summer window but historical issues stalk him too.

Last season’s big money flop Yoane Wissa started this one well and looked ready to fly after starring and scoring in an August win at Spurs.

That was the £50million forward’s last goal, though, and he also only has one assist to his name.

On Saturday in the gutsy draw with Arsenal he came on in the 83rd minute and that spoke volumes.

One player whose career has headed the other way is Aston Villa defender Victor Lindelof.

The Swede was signed on a free from Manchester United largely to make the numbers up in August 2025 but his rise to prominence has been such that Match of the Day were moved to note his absence through injury from the team that drew with Sunderland at Villa Park.

Lindelof is 32 now but has just signed a new contract at Villa. Another one to benefit from Unai Emery’s regenerative elixir.

Unai Emery's coaching magic has helped transform the fortunes of Victor Lindelof

If this weekend has been – in part – about defenders then the Fulham recruitment staff deserve their props too.

The west London club had conceded seven goals in losing their opening three league games before Austrian defender David Affenbruger arrived on the last day of the summer window.

Debuting in the 0-0 draw at Liverpool that followed, Fulham have since lost just one of the seven subsequent games in which he has played.

The fee? £8.5million. Further proof that it really can be done.

Florian Wirtz has credited Andoni Iraola with helping him rediscover his best football at Liverpool after emerging from a difficult period to become one of the Reds’ most influential attacking players.

The German international struggled to consistently reproduce his Bayer Leverkusen form following his £116million move to Anfield in 2025.

However, the picture now looks very different, with Wirtz enjoying an impressive run under Iraola and appearing increasingly comfortable with English football.

Speaking ahead of Liverpool’s Champions League clash with Club Brugge, Wirtz told Liverpool’s official website that Iraola’s confidence has played a major role in his resurgence.

“I’m really enjoying playing under Iraola. He’s a really good coach and has shown that his whole career as a manager”.

“He is bringing me back in a place where I was maybe two years ago where I played really good football, I can feel that he gives me the confidence and I’m really happy about that”.

Wirtz scored and assisted in Liverpool’s emphatic 4-0 victory over Manchester United on Sunday, having also registered a goal and assist against Crystal Palace before the international break.

A CaughtOffside report highlighted just how dominant he was against United. Wirtz created 10 chances from open play, reportedly the highest total by a Premier League player in a single match since David Silva recorded 11 in 2015.

This is exactly what Liverpool supporters expected when Wirtz arrived from Leverkusen.

His talent was never really the issue. Adapting to the Premier League, finding his best position and playing with confidence were bigger obstacles. Iraola appears to have addressed all three.

Wirtz is now operating with greater freedom and combining effectively with Liverpool’s other attacking players, while his improved physical condition and greater familiarity with English football are also helping.

Perhaps most importantly, Iraola trusted him when performances were not producing enough end product.

Liverpool invested heavily because they believed Wirtz could become the creative centrepiece of their attack. They are now beginning to see that player.

If this trajectory continues, Iraola’s biggest achievement at Liverpool may not simply be improving results, it could be turning Wirtz into the Premier League superstar the club always believed they were signing.

Good evening and welcome to our live coverage of this Europa League tie between Bournemouth and AC Milan at the Vitality Stadium.

Back in 2008, Bournemouth’s prospect of a European meeting with Milan seemed impossible. After entering administration with crippling debts of around £4m, Bournemouth were handed a 10-point deduction and relegated from League One. To make matters worse, a hefty 17-point deduction was given to the club ahead of the 2008-09 League Two season, with relegation to non-league seeming inevitable. However, midway through the campaign, the transformative Eddie Howe was parachuted in as Bournemouth’s saviour, eventually guiding the club to safety.

Fast forward to October 2026 in an extraordinary rise and Bournemouth are competing in their first-ever European campaign in the club’s 127-year existence. They welcome Milan to Dorset, having earned back-to-back victories over Real Sociedad and Sturm Graz to kick off their inaugural Europa League adventure in style.

Now, they host the second most successful side in the European Cup history. In terms of heritage and silverware, these clubs could not be further apart, but on the pitch, it’s incredibly tough to call.

On Sunday, Marco Rose’s Bournemouth picked up their first Premier League win of the season, beating 10-man Sunderland 2-0 at the Vitality thanks to goals from Marcus Tavernier and Evanilson to move out of the relegation zone.

Meanwhile, Ruben Amorim is in charge at Milan and returns to England after a tumultuous 14-month reign at Manchester United, where he was sacked in January. Milan lost their opening Europa League fixture 2-0 at home to Benfica, before battering Salzburg 4-0 in Austria, with Alphadjo Cisse netting a stunning hat-trick.

Crystal Palace are also in the Europa League tonight and face an incredibly daunting away trip to Turkish side Besiktas. Pressure is firmly on manager Pierre Sage following the 5-0 humiliation against Brighton last weekend and a shaky start to the season. Palace lost 3-2 to Sage’s former employers Lyon in their previous Europa League outing, with a positive performance and result needed to restore the fans’ faith.

Both games kick-off at 20:00, with team news coming imminently.

#1270. Allegri: ‘Napoli must be realistic against Manchester City’

Max Allegri warns Napoli ‘must be realistic’ about their Champions League chances against Manchester City with a decimated squad. ‘We’ve got to be on our toes and play behind them.’

It kicks off at the Etihad in Manchester at 20.00 GMT (21.00 CET).

You can follow all the build-up and action as it happens from this game and Como vs. AEK Athens on the Champions League Liveblog.

The Partenopei have had a dismal run in Europe so far, scraping the 4-3 victory over Bodo/Glimt, but losing the other three to Arsenal, Villarreal and FC Porto.

This is an incredibly tough trip to Manchester, but will be hoping for better than last season, when Giovanni Di Lorenzo was sent off just 21 minutes into a 2-0 defeat.

“This is a wonderful evening against one of the best teams in Europe, they have very technical, physical players,” Allegri told Sky Sport Italia.

“It is going to be very complicated, we must try to be precise, because they will pounce on any mistake and keep pressure on, and when we do make an error, we’ve got to be on our toes.”

The injury crisis keeps getting worse for Napoli, who make the trip without Antonio Vergara, Benoit Badiashile, Alex Meret, Stanislav Lobotka, Giovanni Di Lorenzo, Alisson Santos, Alessandro Buongiorno and suspended Rafa Marin.

This might be a 3-4-2-1 or a 3-5-1-1, depending on Noa Lang, Kevin De Bruyne and Scott McTominay’s positions, but the coach seemed to hint there will be a lot of long balls and crosses.

“When City press us, we must do well to play behind them, then develop it well. If we don’t, then they will intercept loose passes and go on the counter-attack,” replied Allegri when asked about the system.

Napoli have a famously terrible record on English soil in Europe, never winning here, with just four draws from 12 attempts, and the coach seemed almost resigned to his fate before kick-off.

“We are trying to get some players back to fitness, but these injuries and playing every three days, it’s hard to create any momentum, added Allegri.

“As soon as the fixture list came out, I said we had to be realistic. Only an idiot wouldn’t realise Napoli would gamble for qualification in the last three games. That doesn’t mean we came here expecting to lose, but we also need to prepare for another big game this weekend in Serie A.

“I know you like to talk about identity and all these nice words, but we also have to be realistic. We’re against one of the strongest teams in Europe, who dominated for 10 years and then bought even more strong players.

“Football is at times very simple, if you have the best players, you win games. We will try our best, but we’re down to the bare bones, the same players have to keep going because we don’t have the options to rotate, and barely have time to train.

“We are still in the Champions League, regardless what happens tonight, and this weekend will be a very important match for the future of Napoli.”

Napoli will visit relegation strugglers Sassuolo on Saturday.

#1269. Chelsea star Emmanuel Emegha ROBBED by phone snatcher in London after leaving Stamford Bridge following 4-1 hammering by Leeds

Published: 18:28 EST, 22 November 2026 | Updated: 09:19 EST, 23 November 2026

Chelsea striker Emmanuel Emegha was robbed after leaving Stamford Bridge on Saturday evening, with the 23-year-old Dutchman having scored in his first start for the club.

Despite grabbing the game's first goal while filling in for the injured Joao Pedro, the Blues were beaten 4-1 by Leeds United and booed both at half-time and full-time.

Daily Mail Sport approached Chelsea and the Metropolitan Police on Sunday morning after hearing that the forward's mobile phone had been stolen after he left the stadium the night before.

Neither stood up the information, but Emegha has now confirmed there was an incident, writing in an Instagram post on Sunday night: 'Unfortunately after the game I was robbed. I am okay and thankfully no one was hurt. Thanks for the messages of support.'

Emegha signed for Chelsea from Strasbourg in the summer on a pre-agreement. The transfer fee between the sister sides has never been disclosed. He has won two caps for the Netherlands national team to date.

An interview with Emegha was included in Saturday's match-day programme in which he said: 'I'm a winner, I'm a fighter. I would do anything to win. If I need to block a ball with the front of my face, I will do it.

Emmanuel Emegha has revealed he was robbed on Saturday after Chelsea's 4-1 loss by Leeds

On Sunday, the Chelsea striker revealed the incident had happened to him on Instagram

He put the Blues ahead at Stamford Bridge on Saturday afternoon - his first goal for the club

'I'm quick, I know how to make runs in behind, and I know that I can be a nightmare for all the defenders. Nobody has seen me yet. When my time comes, I will be ready, and I know that the stadium will love my energy.'

It coincided with him being handed his first start for the Blues and scoring his first goal via a nice left-footed finish. However, Chelsea's 1-0 lead lasted only three minutes as Leeds capitalised on suspect defending to equalise, and then deservedly won.

Noah Okafor scored twice, while Dominic Calvert-Lewin and Brenden Aaronson got one goal each.

#1267. University students are biggest spreaders of COVID

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Heidi Ledford reports for Nature from Seattle, Washington.

Undergraduate students on university campuses played a big part in spreading viral variants during the COVID-19 pandemic.Credit: Leonard Ortiz/Digital First Media/Orange County Register/Getty

Universities have become hotbeds of SARS-CoV-2 transmission, according to a massive analysis of more than 85,000 viral genome sequences and other data collected from people with COVID-19.

COVID can wake up a slew of dormant viruses inside you

COVID can wake up a slew of dormant viruses inside you

The study, published on 19 November in the journal Cell1, finds that viral transmission between 2021 and 2023 was highest in adolescents aged 15–18 in schools, undergraduates at university and residents in nursing facilities. Undergraduates, in particular, were consistently the first group to start spreading emerging genetic variants of SARS-CoV-2.

Surprisingly, however, staff members at all three types of institution had about the same risk of contracting COVID-19 as did those in their surrounding communities. So, for example, professors were about as likely to get COVID-19 from the coffee baristas in their university towns as they were to get it from a student at their university.

The analysis is among the largest to bring together viral genomic sequences and medical data from people with COVID-19. “The scale is truly impressive,” says Bill Hanage, who studies the evolution of infectious diseases at the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health in Boston, Massachusetts. “It’s an example of the depth and the detail of the picture that can be painted using the medium of population genomics.”

The findings were based on data collected from COVID-19 tests taken by people in Massachusetts between November 2021 and January 2023. The genomic data allowed researchers to trace the path of SARS-CoV-2 variants that emerged over time, and to link this with epidemiological data about the study participants, such as their age and whether they had been vaccinated against COVID-19.

COVID jabs for kids: they’re safe and they work — so why is uptake so patchy?

COVID jabs for kids: they’re safe and they work — so why is uptake so patchy?

Overall, the team found that booster vaccinations helped to reduce SARS-CoV-2 transmission. This was true even for BA.1, an Omicron variant that started to circulate in Massachusetts in late 2021 — a striking result because COVID-19 vaccines at that time hadn’t yet been updated to protect against BA.1, Hanage says. “That’s an important illustration of how vaccines, even when they’re not perfect, can still be beneficial,” he says.

#1265. Sheepish Man United stars roll into Carrington after 4-0 trouncing at Liverpool as Mauricio Pochettino and Co launch FA appeal against Leny Yoro's 'painful' red card

By OLLIE LEWIS, SPORTS DIGITAL EDITOR and CHRIS WHEELER, NORTHERN SPORTS WRITER

Published: 05:58 EST, 23 November 2026 | Updated: 10:41 EST, 23 November 2026

Mauricio Pochettino hauled his beleaguered Man United stars back into Carrington early on Monday morning after the new manager's chastening Anfield bow on Sunday.

Pochettino, who replaced Michael Carrick last week, was served a sobering reality check at the hands of United's fierce rivals Liverpool, with the Red Devils on the receiving end of a 4-0 trouncing on Merseyside.

The Argentine bemoaned the impact of what he described as a harsh red card against defender Leny Yoro in the opening eight minutes of the contest, but admitted he has plenty to do to turn things around - with United stuck in 19th in the Premier League table.

And Pochettino had his players check in for training early on Monday morning, with a downcast Bruno Fernandes and his team-mates spotted arriving at around 8.30am - roughly an hour earlier than under Carrick.

Under Carrick's stewardship, players were given the day after a game off, and it remains to be seen whether Pochettino will do away with that approach in favour of a recovery day at the club's training ground - a similar approach to that taken by former United boss Ruben Amorim.

Man United stars were ordered back into training on Monday after their trouncing at Anfield

Matthijs de Ligt cut a contemplative figure as he drove through the gates at Carrington

Director of football Jason Wilcox continues to have questions to answer after Man United were unable to elevate themselves out of the relegation zone

News also came on Monday that Man United are appealing to the FA over Yoro’s controversial red card.

Yoro was sent off in the eighth minute for a challenge on Alexander Isak on the edge of the penalty box. The Frenchman was dismissed by referee Sam Barrott, and Dominik Szoboszlai scored Liverpool’s first goal from the free kick as 10-man United were thrashed 4-0.

However, United insist that Yoro did not deny Isak a clear goalscoring opportunity because goalkeeper Senne Lammens would have reached the ball first.

The club have notified the FA of their intention to appeal in the hope of having Yoro’s one-match ban overturned so he can play against Brentford at Old Trafford on Saturday.

In September, Pro Ref boss Howard Webb apologised to United when Erling Haaland’s winning goal for Manchester City in the Old Trafford derby was allowed to stand after VAR incorrectly ruled that teammate Enzo Fernandez was not interfering with play as he tried to head the ball in an offside position.

Last season, Webb acknowledged that the match officials got it wrong when they decided not to send off Brentford captain Nathan Collins for hauling back Bryan Mbeumo inside the box as United lost 3-1 at the Gtech Community Stadium.

New United head coach Pochettino blamed Yoro’s red card for the heavy defeat in his first game in charge, and was unhappy that Barrott took no action over a similar incident involving Jeremy Jacquet and Mbeumo in the Liverpool penalty area moments earlier.

'So painful, so disappointed,' said the Argentine. 'It's not OK to start a game in the Premier League with this situation. The game changed completely after eight minutes. Now we can explain everything, but the damage is done – it's so painful.

'It's clear that after eight minutes the plan was in the bin. Do you think that is easy? Even the best team in the world playing in this situation concedes four goals or maybe more.

'We are not going to lose more than one game how we lost today. I take the responsibility, and we keep pushing.

'We feel pain for this defeat, but we need to keep our heads up and translate that anger into energy to start to work from tomorrow for the next game.

'We are in a situation that this is very complicated. It's difficult, yes, but I think we fight, we made the effort, and I know how they feel now in the dressing-room.

'The players are feeling the pain of the result. I told them to be calm: it was an unfair situation that happened. We need to accept that reality. We need to try to increase our focus, concentration and make better decisions on the field.

'We also need to be critical on ourselves but some situations happened in the game that we are not happy.'

But more critical were former Red Devils Roy Keane and Gary Neville, both of whom were pushed to extremes assessing the match after the final whistle.

Lisandro Martinez was among the Man United defenders that Gary Neville did not feel were up to the task at Anfield

But incoming manager Pochettino was keen to place the majority of blame on the harsh red card doled out to Leny Yoro

Neville was driven to slapping his face in the Sky Sports studio to demonstrate Man United's defenders' lack of hunger and poise.

'I never see any of them on their toes, alert, looking like they've got something fixed in here', he said before pointing to his head.

'I never see any of them look like that,' he added. 'They look like that -'

Neville then stared into the middle distance for a few moments to share the blankness he sees on the faces of the back line, before spitting: 'Wake up!'

The Overlap broadcaster slapped himself a number of times while repeating 'wake up!' and adding: 'You play for Man United'.

Keane was pushed to the brink of swearing in his snap description of the team's performance, adding that he thought Neville's verdict - that the 4-0 scoreline might have been worse under the circumstances - took players off the hook.

'If I hear that one more time from the lads in the commentary that 4-0 is not too bad when you're down to 10 men - has a team ever got a result with 10 men before?' Keane said immediately after the final whistle. 'It can be done.

'I thought United were desperate. I thought they were so bad and everyone and Nev, who played for Man United saying 4-0 ain't bad.'

'(The red card) doesn't help but you're telling me they couldn't have done better? They lost 4-0 with 10 men, that's not too bad? Has a team ever got a result with 10 men? It can be done. At least show a bit more fight, a bit more quality - I can't believe what I'm hearing from people.

'You played for the club, saying 4-0 isn't too bad. Wow. Fans are applauding. Applauding what? Performing rubbish. Liverpool were excellent, but how easy did United make it for them? I can't believe what I'm watching sometimes.

'This team two years ago finished 15th. The last year or two, we're talking. We're blaming the board, blaming ownership, blaming managers.

'When do the players take responsibility for some decision-making? Liverpool probably should have scored eight, probably eight or nine, unbelievable chances they had. And everyone's coming off the pitch saying 4 is not too bad? I feel like swearing.'
