#1123. Harry Potter films turns 25 ahead of new TV series' release

In 2001, "Harry Potter and the Sorcerer's Stone" hit cinemas and took the world by storm. Today, anticipation for the new series is high, but its creator, J.K. Rowling, remains a controversial figure.

On November 4, 2001, London's Leicester Square became a world of witches and wizards. The occasion was the world premiere of "Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone" (released in the US and India as "Harry Potter and the Sorcerer's Stone").

"Thousands of excited fans, some dressed up in wizard hats and cloaks, gathered to catch a glimpse of arriving celebrities," the BBC reported at the time.

Daniel Radcliffe, who played Harry Potter, was just 12 years old and clearly impressed by the spectacle. The BBC quoted him as saying, "It is so cool. I have never heard my name shouted so much in an hour."

The crowds showed just how far Harry Potter fever had spread in only four years.

The first Harry Potter book was published by Britain's Bloomsbury in June 1997, with an initial print run of just 500 hardcover copies.

About 5,000 paperback copies were also released around the same time.

Today, first editions are prized collectors' items, with hardcover copies commanding high prices at auction. In mid-October, one sold for $400,000 through US auction house Heritage Auctions.

At first, the book's popularity grew largely by word of mouth among schoolchildren. Media attention followed when it won the prestigious Nestle Smarties Book Prize later that year.

With an estimated 120 million-plus copies sold worldwide, it is the best-selling book in the series and ranks among the best-selling novels of all time.

For years, J.K. Rowling's public image was defined by her extraordinary rise from a single mother on welfare to a billionaire.

But in recent years, debate over her views on gender and transgender identity has increasingly overshadowed that success. It's an issue Rowling herself frequently weighs in on.

In an essay published on her website on October 21, 2026, Rowling reiterated her opposition to what she calls the "current, dominant strain of trans activism." She argues that this movement "holds that a man who declares himself a woman is, literally, a woman, and is therefore entitled to be treated as a woman in all contexts." Rowling argues that allowing trans women into single-sex spaces poses a risk. She describes biological sex as an indisputable biological fact.

Such statements have led critics to accuse Rowling of transphobia, while others regard her stance as a defense of women's rights and safety.

The controversy has also divided her fans. Some stand by Rowling, while others try to draw a distinction between the books and their author.

Others have left Harry Potter behind altogether. One former fan is German YouTuber Coldmirror, known for her Harry Potter parodies. The media artist from the Bremen area, whose real name is Kathrin Fricke, told the Süddeutsche Zeitung newspaper: "I don't have any love left for Harry. I'm still somewhat interested, but I can no longer watch it in good conscience." She cited Rowling's campaigning against transgender people as the reason.

The "Harry Potter" film cast is divided as well. The three main stars — Daniel Radcliffe, Emma Watson and Rupert Grint — have publicly spoken out in support of transgender people. Meanwhile, Ralph Fiennes, who played Lord Voldemort, and Helena Bonham Carter, who portrayed Bellatrix Lestrange, have defended Rowling's right to express her views.

Despite the controversy surrounding Rowling, Warner Bros., which holds the Harry Potter film rights, is bringing the books back to the screen — this time as a series for HBO. The premiere is scheduled for December 25.

The eight-episode first season is an an adaption of the first book. Even though the episode lengths haven't been announced, the scope of a TV series gives each book much more room than the original films did. That means more time to explore subplots, character development and everyday life at Hogwarts. While many fans are looking forward to a more detailed adaptation, others remain skeptical. They find it hard to imagine the familiar characters being played by anyone else.

The new trio consists of Dominic McLaughlin as Harry Potter, Arabella Stanton as Hermione Granger and Alastair Stout as Ron Weasley.

J.K. Rowling is an executive producer on the show. HBO says, however, that her views on gender identity won't be reflected in the storyline. Several people involved in the new production have publicly distanced themselves from her views. Paapa Essiedu, who has been cast as Severus Snape, signed an open letter supporting transgender people. Rowling subsequently said she had neither the power nor the desire to have him removed from the show because of it. John Lithgow, who plays Dumbledore, and Nick Frost, who portrays Hagrid, have also spoken out against Rowling's views.

Meanwhile, the Harry Potter merchandising machine is still going strong. On November 4, Britain's largest Harry Potter store to date is set to open in London. According to Warner Bros., the two-story shop covers more than 1,950 square meters.

This article was originally written in German.

#1122. Cavan Sullivan wins MLS Young Player of the Year as league announces award winners and finalists

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

With the MLS Cup playoffs now in full swing, it also means that we are beginning to see who is taking home honors at the end of the season. Nashville SC have already seen Maxwell Woledzi win Defender of the Year and Bran Shwake earn Goalkeeper of the Year honors, and they have potential honorees up and down the awards docket alongside the youngest MVP finalist in league history, Cavan Sullivan, who has taken home young player of the year honors. Antoine Griezmann has also won Newcomer of the Year in only half of a season with Orlando City SC.

Check out the winners and finalists so far:

Leading Nashville SC to a record low of 25 goals conceded and tying Tony Meola's record for the most clean sheets in an MLS season with 16, Brian Schwake has taken home Goalkeeper of the Year honors by a landslide, beating out finalists Matt Turner and Roman Bürki. In only his first season as the full-time starter for Nashville, Schwake took the reins and didn't look back, also debuting for the U.S. Men's National Team due to his success. He also set club records for wins, penalty kick saves (three), save percentage (78.4%), and goals against average (0.76).

It's astounding that Eduard Lowen is playing soccer, considering what the few years have looked like for him. In March of this year, his wife Ilona died from brain cancer after they managed through her diagnosis, with Lowen taking time off from the game to support her and her family. He returned to MLS play in April, scoring in his first start of the season for St. Louis City SC, but then was traded to San Jose after the World Cup break. During that time with San Jose, he became an important part of their playoff run with one goal and three assists.

Becoming the youngest MVP finalist in league history at only 17, it should come as no surprise that Cavan Sullivan has won Young Player of the Year, beating out the Red Bull New York duo of Julian Hall and Adri Mehmeti. During the World Cup break, Sullivan spent time training with the Union's MLS Next Pro side instead of taking the time off for himself, and the results showed in the second half of the season as he helped lead the Union into a playoff spot. With nine goals and 14 assists (including secondary assists), no teenager has ever been involved in more goals in a season than Sullivan, and it has also led to his first cap with the United States men's national team, where he was able to grab his first goal against Mexico. If this is the tip of the iceberg, we're in for something special, considering that this has been a banner year for young players in MLS, with more minutes being given to teenagers than ever before. The future is in good hands as the kids are leveling up each day.

With Guilherme receiving MVP votes to become a finalist for the award, it was going to take a special performance for someone else to win Newcomer of the Year, and joining Orlando City SC, Antoine Griezmann did just that. Prior to his arrival, this was a team floundering below the playoff line after moving on from manager Oscar Pareja. In only a half-season, he came in and scored 14 goals and assisted eight more as the first player ever to produce 20 goal contributions in only half a season, while turning this team into contenders. It's going to be tough in the playoffs for Griezmann to overcome the defense, but considering what he has already done with the squad, there's no reason why Orlando should be counted out with the Frenchman next to Justin Ellis.

En route to setting a points record with 77 points to win the Supporters' Shield, Nashville SC were also led by a record-setting defense that only let the ball into the back of the net 25 times in an entire campaign. That success was rewarded with all three finalists for Defender of the Year coming from Nashville, but it's their newest signing that took home the award. Joining from Norwegian club Fredrikstad ahead of the season, Woledzi didn't need much time to adjust, appearing in every regular-season match and helping Nashville build from the back to maintain possession. It was a team effort to tie the MLS clean sheet record with 17 during the season, so it's only natural for one of their defenders to get the honors this season.

#1120. Gold for the West Bank: Meet Palestinian karate champ Mariam Bsharat

The occupied West Bank is not an obvious breeding ground for sporting success. But Mariam Bsharat, 17, has beaten the odds to become a karate world champion and is making a new life in Germany.

"After the referee lifted my hand to show I'm now a two-time world champion, it was a very overwhelming feeling," Mariam Bsharat said. "Making history once is something, but making it twice is really something else. I felt very happy and I felt a big relief. Only I know how many sacrifices I made and how many hardships I needed to overcome."

Themes of relief, joy and sacrifice are commonplace in the reflections of athletes after a big win. In Mariam Bsharat's case, it's about more than just dedication to training and taking care of the body. The 17-year-old won her second under-21 World Karate Championship gold medal competing for the Palestine national team in Poland in October.

"It was everyday life, seeing people get killed around me and houses getting bombed," she told DW of her upbringing in the occupied West Bank.

"I faced challenges in transportation," Bsharat said. "I wasn't able to go from one city to another to be able to train with other people, so that I can actually prepare for competitions. I needed to travel to other countries like Jordan or Egypt ... which was very hard for me. And, financially, the support wasn't really the support an elite athlete needed."

Growing up in Nablus, Bsharat had a narrow path to the top. But initially, it was her own reluctance that threatened to stop a champion career before it started.

"When I was a little kid, I did not really love it," said Bsharat, who competes in the division for fighters who weigh under 66 kilograms (145 pounds).

"I started it because my family was in that sport," Bsharat said. "My father had a dojo, and my mother also did that sport. My siblings and my aunts and my uncles — it's a family thing. I started it because they were all doing it. In time, I started getting into it."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Family has been a constant source of comfort and inspiration for Bsharat. Her father and uncle have acted as manager and coach respectively. While her mother and siblings moved with Mariam to Hamburg, Germany, last year, her father remained in order to take care of his business, the dojo, though he visits and tries to be with his daughter in competitions. Integration has been made easier by her mastery of the language, taught to her by her German mother.

Bsharat has mixed feelings about leaving her homeland.

"I'm thankful to be here because being in Germany opened lot of doors for me, and I think I have a brighter future here," Bsharat said. "But also being in Palestine was just my everyday life, and I loved it there. My family was around me, my friends were around me, and I just felt comfortable, which was a big change coming here to Germany. I think every change comes with hardships."

As well as the obvious difficulties of living in an area occupied by Israel, there are particular challenges for sportspeople living in the West Bank and the Gaza Strip, with access to facilities, travel and constant security fears among them. As such, very few people from the Palestinian territories become successful on the international sporting stage. That, Bsharat said, gives her responsibilities that are unusual and heavy for a person of any age, let alone a 17-year-old.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"Being an elite athlete in Palestine is something very special because not everybody in Palestine has that opportunity. There aren't really a lot of athletes that are elite and who win international medals,” Bsharat said.

"So all that pressure from all the country and all the people, the family, the coaches are on me because I'm representing them, raising their flag,” she said. "I sometimes even forget to fight for myself and actually think about myself."

That has not yet proved a barrier to Bsharat, who is is ranked first in the world in her category by the World Karate Federation (WKF). With Palestine recognized by the International Olympic Committee, Bsharat would likely have been a contender to raise that flag in Los Angeles at the 2028 Olympics. But the sport was dropped from the Games in 2024.

"The global karate community remains steadfast in our belief that the natural place for karate is within the Olympic Games, and we sincerely hope that the incongruence we suffered in Paris 2024 and LA 2028 will be corrected for Brisbane 2032, if not sooner," the WKF wrote in response to the decision in 2024. The sport was also taken off the slate for the recent Youth Games in Senegal.

Should karate return in Brisbane, Bsharat would likely be approaching her prime. In the meantime, she is looking forward to starting her journey as a senior when she turns 18. But she won't be hanging around.

"My goal is it to be a world champion at seniors, which is the hardest and the best thing you can achieve in karate," she said.

"But winning an Olympic medal, being called Olympic champion or just representing my country with that flag [is a thought that] is just full of happiness and pride."

The interview was conducted by Janek Speight.

#1119. Alejandro Garnacho's nightmare Aston Villa loan continues: Struggling star is left at home as Unai Emery picks TWO goalkeepers on bench for Galatasaray defeat before sending warning to ex-Man United winger

Published: 17:00 EST, 24 November 2026 | Updated: 17:05 EST, 24 November 2026

Alejandro Garnacho's future at Aston Villa was plunged into further doubt on Tuesday as he was overlooked for their defeat at Galatasaray.

The Argentine joined on loan from Chelsea last summer with a £43million obligation to buy, triggered when certain targets were hit.

Yet Garnacho has yet to start for Villa and was not even on the bench in Istanbul, even though two goalkeepers were named.

Asked whether Garnacho was fit for this match, Villa boss Unai Emery said: 'Today I think the best players to play with us, to be with us, were here.'

Daily Mail Sport has reported regularly this season that Garnacho may not see out his loan spell and now that looks increasingly likely to be the case.

There is not thought to be a break clause in the loan but if Chelsea and Villa agreed to cancel it, that would allow Garnacho to go elsewhere in January.

Alejandro Garnacho was not in the Aston Villa squad for their defeat at Galatasaray on Tuesday

Villa boss Unai Emery chose to include two goalkeepers on his bench instead of picking of him

Villa had a similar situation with Harvey Elliott. The midfielder joined on loan from Liverpool in summer 2025 but barely played.

Emery decided quickly that he did not want to sign Elliott permanently and could not risk triggering the appearance clause that would have seen him join Villa for £35m.

Villa are now without a win in six and Emery admitted: 'The next challenge against PSG at home will be huge. If we can recover the three points we lost today maybe we still have a chance to reach the top eight but we are not favourites.'

Emery also bemoaned the home side's time-wasting tactics after Deniz Gul headed them into a 77th-minute lead.

He said: 'I am not blaming the referee but he was unfair with us by adding only five minutes. After they scored it was impossible to play.'

#1118. Nicolò Tresoldi: Why 2027 could change everything with a likely transfer and a career-defining decision ahead

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

There is a new talent in Europe who will make his name in the near future, and that's Nicolò Tresoldi. The 22-year-old is currently playing for Club Brugge and on October 13 scored three goals at San Siro against Inter, showing the world he's ready for the next step in his career. 2027 will be a pivotal year in Tresoldi's career, not only because he could be on the verge of a move to a bigger European club, but also because he may have to make a definitive decision about his international future. With Germany, Italy and Argentina all potentially in the picture, choosing which national team to represent could prove just as significant as his next club move.

When Tresoldi, the son of a former Serie A player, scored the hat-trick against Inter at San Siro, all the headlines were about his childhood and his love for AC Milan, the Nerazzurri's biggest rival, who, according to reports, are also in talks to potentially sign him in the future. But just how special is Tresoldi, and which European giants could be in the running to sign him in 2027?

Nicolò Tresoldi silences the San Siro 🤫Club Brugge stun Inter 🥶 pic.twitter.com/D8TIEn6b9C

Tresoldi was born in Cagliari, Sardinia, in 2004, during the summer months when his family would regularly spend time on the island. His connection to Sardinia stemmed from his maternal grandfather, who worked there as a golf instructor. Thanks to this family connection, they had a house on the island and would spend part of their summers there, but because of his mother's job, he moved with his family to Hannover in 2017, when he was 13.

Tresoldi, who until then had played tennis more regularly, decided to start his soccer career in the Hannover academy, where he debuted with the second team before making his first-team debut in 2022. He immediately drew interest from multiple European clubs, and in the summer of 2025 he joined Club Brugge in Belgium, his first major move as a professional soccer player. In his first season at the club, he scored 23 goals in 58 games, including four in the Champions League's league phase, and he has started his second season even better, with 15 goals in all competitions so far, including that unforgettable hat-trick against Inter in Milan.

Next year will also be the year he makes a final decision about which national team he wants to represent. Tresoldi is eligible for Germany, Italy and Argentina. In 2023, he decided to join the German U21 team, and he now intends to see out the entire cycle through the 2027 U21 European Championship, which will take place in the summer. Until then, he won't make a final decision, but both Italy coach Roberto Mancini and Germany coach Jürgen Klopp have expressed interest in calling him up.

Speaking on the topic and about Tresoldi's future, Klopp said: "It doesn't mean that he has made a decision against Germany or Italy. We don't want to put any pressure on the players. It's a sensitive matter, and we will respect whatever decision he makes, without rushing him." Mancini, on the other hand, seemed more optimistic about him choosing Italy: "I've spoken to Tresoldi myself. He needs to feel that he wants to represent our national team. Given that he was born in Italy and has an Italian father, I believe there is a possibility. We hope he makes the right choice; he knows how much he would mean to us." Argentina can also hope to call him up, as his mother is from there, and he could be included in Lionel Scaloni's squad. However, Italy and Germany are his most likely choices.

Before that, he will also be the subject of transfer rumors starting in the early months of the new year, as many top European clubs are looking for a new striker. AC Milan have to be on that list, as the Rossoneri will likely sign a new striker to play alongside Gonçalo Ramos, even though Club Brugge reportedly value him at around $50 million. At the same time, we need to monitor what Bayern Munich do in the January transfer window, as Harry Kane's injury might force the German side to change strategy in the short term. For sure, 2027 will be the year of Tresoldi, as he now focuses his attention on two moves that will shape his future.

#1117. Newcastle fans turn on Jaissle as defeat triggers relegation concerns

Newcastle United did not just lose to Everton, they lost the home crowd, whose enthusiasm to back their team has drained from them at alarming speed.

This was a performance that belonged in the pre-takeover era, those bad old days under Steve McClaren, John Carver and Steve Bruce. It was a hugely satisfying evening for Everton manager David Moyes, who insisted there was “a way back” for Jack Grealish, even though he was once again left at home after he missed training last week without permission.

The atmosphere went flat early and gradually turned into anger and frustration. The crowd initially tried to stay with their team but were repeatedly punched in the face by the grim reality of the spectacle in front of them. They do not like the style of play, they do not like the application of the players and they cannot accept the results. They are fed up with pretending otherwise.

This was another miserable performance from Matthias Jaissle’s side, who did not manage a shot on target until the 86th minute. He has only been in the job three months, but nothing seems to be getting better.

“I have to take the responsibility,” he said. “We did not transfer the things we did in training. Hitting long balls all the time, that was not the plan. We were not brave enough to play short passes.

“As soon as the referee blew his whistle, the plan disappeared. We could feel the anger and the frustration, I felt it on the touchline. We are low on confidence and it shows.”

Newcastle looked listless, clueless and alarmingly devoid of belief in what they were being asked to do. They have the unmistakable whiff of a team in decline.

If they do not start playing a lot better, they will be worried about a relegation battle. It is four defeats in their last five games and the confidence in Jaissle to find solutions is fading. Rather than change what he is asking his team to do, he has doubled down on the formation and tactics.

Concerns have been creeping steadily upwards since August. There is a lack of confidence in the players, and worries about the quality of the eight new signings made over the summer.

In particular, there are serious misgivings about the implementation of the “vertical football” Jaissle has imported to the North East of England from the Austro-German Red Bull coaching school.

A night under the lights at St James’ Park should be a boisterous affair, but things went flat quickly. Newcastle, as they have tended to do this season, resorted to long balls punted forward. More often than not they were poorly directed – only 22 per cent were accurate over 98 minutes.

There was no fluency and no threat. The first groans were heard inside 15 minutes as another pass was hoisted harmlessly into the air. They grew more widespread and more frequent.

Everton, just as they had in their Carabao Cup win last week, looked comfortable. Recognising how easy it was to nullify Newcastle’s game plan, they offered an attacking threat of their own.

A rising shot from Merlin Röhl briefly had goalkeeper Lukas Hornicek worried. A free-kick into the Newcastle box caused panic. James Tarkowski won the first header, but Thierno Barry swung and missed with his left foot.

The groans began to turn into boos and whistles. Jaissle’s side could barely string more than two passes together. It felt precarious.

This is not an easy place to play football when the crowd airs its displeasure. As the first half limped on, there were players in black and white who looked like they could not handle the pressure.

It was a horrible game of football. With the last kick of the half, Everton should have taken the lead, Harrison Armstrong picked out Barry inside the box, but he made a mess of the finish. The referee’s whistle was accompanied by boos and a scream of “sort it out” from behind Jaissle’s technical area.

He did not follow those blunt instructions. Everton took the lead in such simple fashion and all Jaissle and his coaching staff could do was shake their heads at each other. Tyrique George was played in far too easily from a free-kick but his shot should have been saved by Hornicek. It was straight at the Czech, but it went through him and it left Barry with a tap in. Newcastle appealed for both a foul on Fabian Schar and an offside but got neither.

#1115. What the Democrats' midterms win means for the US economy and Trump

From high oil prices and data centers to tariffs and mounting debt, economic concerns played a key role in the crushing defeat of President Donald Trump's Republicans. So can the Democrats now make a difference?

For the millions who cast their ballots in the US midterm elections, one issue ranked above all others: the economy.

So what does the Democrats' stunning capture of both the US Senate and House of Representatives mean for the economy and economic policy, given that President Donald Trump still has two years of his term to go?

Markets have rebounded after initially trending negatively. Global stocks rallied as investors appeared to take heart from the Democrats' victory.

With Democrats now holding comfortable majorities in both houses of Congress and Trump still in the White House, it could lead to gridlock in Washington. Trump has already said he would become "Mr Veto," meaning he would block any legislation the Democrats advance.

"The magnitude of the gains for the Democrats in the midterms does not change too much for the near-term policy outlook, given the party still lacks a filibuster-proof majority in the Senate and President Trump has veto power to block legislation," Stephen Brown, chief North America economist with Capital Economics, said in a note.

"I think we are looking at two years of complete 100% gridlock," Jacob Funk Kirkegaard, nonresident senior fellow with the Peterson Institute for International Economics, told DW after the results came in. "Nothing will get done of any kind."

Some investors appear worried that the Democrats could force through AI regulation, especially if they also win the White House in 2028. Rising opposition among large majorities of the US population to data centers — the key infrastructure behind AI — helped secure victories for many Democratic candidates.

Kirkegaard, who is also a senior fellow at Bruegel, a European economics think tank, said the vote showed the extent of that opposition.  Even if the Democrats can't force regulation, he thinks local opposition will make it harder for data centers to be built, which could hit the valuation of big tech firms that have benefitted from the AI boom.

"This election shows that the political underpinning of the rapid, aggressive AI growth story is shaky," he said. "It doesn't mean it's going to stop or be made illegal, but the dynamic of the growth story has shifted."

If the Democrats were to win the presidency in 2028, Brown said, they would be perfectly placed to make major policy changes. "That includes the potential for tax hikes on corporations and high-income individuals as well as regulation that could delay the AI rollout," he said.

According to polling conducted in early October by the Pew Research Center, 56% of Americans say Trump's tariff policies will have mostly negative impacts on the country, with only 20% saying mostly positive.

That sentiment clearly drove many Democrats to victory in the midterms — particularly in states where tariffs have had a particularly negative impact. That includes those with sectors reliant on exports, such as Texas, Michigan, Iowa and Illinois, where counter-tariffs have hit and those that have high trade volumes with Canada.

Yet, barring an unprecedented climbdown from Trump — who has been ideologically wedded to tariffs since he first became a public figure almost 50 years ago — it's not clear how the Democrats could force substantial change to the president's signature economic policy.

"Trump will not be moderated," Deborah Elms, head of trade policy at the Hinrich Foundation in Singapore, told DW earlier this year. "Expect him to continue his trade disruption and tariff policies for as long as he remains in the Oval Office."

Though the US Constitution gives Congress the power to collect and organize tariffs, various laws passed over the years have given presidents power to implement tariffs when they cite certain conditions, such as national security or economic emergencies.

Trump has already used such avenues for his tariffs and can continue to do so, despite some legal rebukes. However, while Congress can't necessarily force an end to Trump's existing tariffs, it can now take further legal action against them to prevent greater escalation.

Though Trump and the Democrats are clearly not going to make common cause, Kirkegaard said, the scale of the Republicans' defeat might force Trump to be less erratic in his policymaking, from escalating his trade war with Canada to his Iran policy.

Trump said in the aftermath of Tuesday's defeats that he would "work with" the Democrats and told the Financial Times in the run-up to the vote that he was unlikely to escalate the war in Iran.

Were a deal to be struck with Iran, soaring energy prices — a pivotal election issue — could finally fall, helping voters with their cost-of-living concerns.

"You've got to get a deal with Iran, and you've got to bring down gas prices," Kirkegaard said. "From a political point of view, that's the most important thing now."

George Saravelos, an analyst with Deutsche Bank FX Research, thinks the markets are beginning to become more optimistic in that area. "With oil flows through the Middle East having materially recovered, the market is pricing a large imminent risk premium of re-escalation and energy supply disruption," he said in a note.

Despite the scale of the Democrats' victory, the fact that Trump remains in the Oval Office will complicate all efforts to force a change to signature economic policies and issues.

Yet Congress can now exert considerable pressure. Another issue vital to voters was corruption and the belief that the Trump administration has engaged in corruption and personal enrichment while in office.

That raises the prospect of the new Democratic-controlled Congress launching legal investigations and potentially pursuing another impeachment of Trump, which could force the president to negotiate on some economic issues to secure his political survival.

"Can you find 10 or 12 Republican senators who, in the face of overwhelming corruption, would be willing to vote for articles of impeachment? I wouldn't rule it out," Kirkegaard said. "And that's a scenario in which Trump might suddenly be much more accommodating to, for instance, abandoning most of his tariffs."

Despite voters' clear rejection of Trump's economic policies, the Democratic Party's newly minted senators, congressmen and congresswomen face an uphill battle in trying to reverse them.

#1114. Why are Arsenal throwing away leads? Itchy trigger fingers cost Mikel Arteta's side against Dortmund

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

LONDON -- To lose one elegantly-earned lead, Mr. Arteta, may be regarded as a misfortune; to lose two looks like carelessness. Three days after frittering away their lead at Newcastle, Arsenal repeated in the Champions League, as Borussia Dortmund became the first team to stop Mikel Arteta's side from winning a league phase game at the Emirates Stadium.

The real impact of two points dropped tonight probably won't become clear until February and the draw for the last 16. A year ago, topping the league table set Arsenal on a favorable path to the Champions League final. There are, of course, no guarantees that they would not get that as a lower seed but a repeat finish in the top two looks unlikely, with Real Madrid and Paris Saint-Germain both in possession of 100% records.

Of more immediate concern for Arteta, who was unstinting in his praise of Arsenal's "brilliant performance", is that this team's very good football is not enough to overwhelm their opposition. It is worth noting, at this early juncture, that this team did position itself to potentially overwhelm the German league leaders. As is so often the case with the Gunners, we're assessing them against standards that would be considered unreasonable for 99% of teams. Usually, when you put up 2.2 xG on Borussia Dortmund and give up 0.9, you can be as pleased with your side as Arteta was in public. In private, you can rest assured that he will be as detail-obsessed as this column in attempting to explain why such sustained spells of excellence still end in a share of the points.

As at St. James' Park on Saturday night, for 45 minutes here, Arsenal were delicious, a true smorgasbord of footballing delights. Piero Hincapie popping up as an additional center forward, Christos Tzolis gliding off the left, Declan Rice barnstorming from third center back to second attacking midfielder in the space of a single pressing trigger.

Borussia Dortmund arrived in north London tied with their hosts for the fewest goals conceded in Europe's top five leagues. Niko Kovac's back five, with three robust midfielders ahead of them, looked like it should be enough to stifle the Gunners. Instead, they were overwhelmed, pulled here and there in their attempts to track position-lite red shirts.

Arsenal's excellence got the goal it deserved, a larruping strike from Viktor Gyokeres that moved one way, then the other, with such extravagance you rather wondered if the Australian cricket team had given the ball a going over beforehand. Nico Schlotterbeck seemed convinced he'd got an edge on it. Gregor Kobel looked dumbfounded. Even Gyokeres' belated donning of the Bane mask suggested he thought there had been some external force aiding him. Not so. You just hit it that well, Viktor.

From there, Arsenal had all they needed to wrap this game up in style. Their press constricted the game into the spaces where Martin Odegaard could excel. Noni Madueke was even more menacing, a player who seems to have unlocked himself in little over a month. They kept getting into the final third. They kept getting shots, too, 14 of them before the half was out. The problem was how bad those shots were. A baker's dozen and one spare and Arsenal couldn't put up a full expected goal before the break.

Too often, moves ended prematurely because someone in red fancied taking a swing from range. Eight of their first-half shots were from outside the box. Gyokeres tried a few heat checks; come the final whistle, he was as cold as the north London night. Declan Rice has evidently read Arteta saying that he should try more shots from range. The ones from outside the box, one of which really brought the oohs as it flew over the bar, weren't even his worst. Not squaring for Madueke in the first half or Gyokeres in the second really was a spurning of prime opportunities.

If this rush to shoot from range were a one-off, you could frame it as Arteta did in his post-match press conference, "a variation in relation to the opponent, the situation that you have". And yet Arsenal have been trying from range more frequently this season, from fewer than four shots per game in 2025-26 to nearly five this term, a 23% increase in shot volume from range. Against Newcastle, the proportions were lower but twice in an excellent 45 minutes, they shot when they could have worked the ball into a better spot. Arteta has spoken about unlocking the long-range potential of his team. Those who know his thinking often frame his obsession with adding "gamechangers" to his roster in terms of players who can beat a man and strike one from deep.

They still take a lower proportion of efforts from outside the box than most teams in Europe's top five leagues but most teams in Europe's top five leagues don't employ Martin Odegaard. For now, the sample size and the variation might be so small as to be explained through happenstance or circumstances rather than design. Bukayo Saka's injury has removed one of Arsenal's primary penalty-box threats from this team. His replacement, Madueke, is still honing his shot profile, if we're being generous.

There is also value to a team that faces so many low blocks proving themselves to be willing to strike from range. Fail to close down an Eberechi Eze and you might well be picking the ball out of your net soon after. Get those defenders moving out of position to close down the shot and an angle to a better opening might present itself.

It is a hard balance to strike. Tonight, Arsenal did not quite manage it: prime positions turned into subprime shots because trigger fingers got itchy.

A driving run from Joane Gadou took him away from Christos Tzolis, as the midfield busied themselves with other matters. Maximilian Beier received the ball in the box and smartly turned away from Gabriel before drilling low past Kepa Arrizabalaga. Even a defense as excellent as Arsenal's can't keep your average Premier League or Champions League opponent from clicking once. The levels are just too high.

An upswing in pressure in the final 35 minutes brought enough moments to leave Arteta baffled. "There is an element of luck here because how in hell some of the goals they haven't gone in, I don't know. Some of the days last year we hit somebody and it was an own goal.

"Quality sometimes [is missing], or [there is a] rush, or [a need] to have a bit of composure, or to read the next pass a little bit better; the execution can be better, but everything that is in between that, I think was really, really good."

He is not wrong. It just seems even more careless to let two points slip away because they could not quell their shot-first instincts.

#1109. Man Utd show fight on night of chaos to give Carrick a glimpse of hope

So maybe there is some fight left in the old dog yet?

At half-time, Manchester United looked down and out and Michael Carrick’s reign as manager as good as finished.

Roma were 2-0 in front and coasting, gorging on a desperate United’s litany of errors, and there was full-scale mutiny in the stands at Old Trafford. A fifth defeat in six matches and the club’s longest winless run for 48 years beckoned. It was toxic on and off the pitch.

And then something changed. United, from being a dishevelled, disorganised mess, suddenly seemed to remember who they were supposed to be and what they were supposed to represent. Surrender gave way to fight. A team that had been feeling sorry for themselves discovered some pride. A crowd that had been baying for blood turned Old Trafford into a bear pit of a very different kind, and Roma simply did not know what had hit them.

This club have served up some famous comebacks over the decades, but it was hard to think of too many occasions when the mood and momentum had shifted this violently from one half to the next.

United fans were in open revolt in that first half, releasing green and gold balloons in protests before kick-off and then throwing tennis balls on to the pitch amid furious chanting against the Glazers and Sir Jim Ratcliffe. The players looked like they would rather have been anywhere else.

And yet by the 86th minute Matheus Cunha’s wild celebrations were encapsulating a wild night, the Brazilian ripping off his shirt after his dramatic winner before launching himself into a delirious crowd drunk on the euphoria of a victory that had seemed improbable in the extreme at the interval, when boos cascaded from the stands.

Whether this proves little more than a thrilling, heroic interlude in the endgame for Carrick, or the start of a genuine turnaround, is hard to know. And, let’s be clear, there was so much about the first-half performance to concern the hierarchy, who came under persistent, furious attack from fans at war with an ownership it reviles and wants gone.

But the second half stood firmly at odds with the shambolic display that had preceded it and suggested all may not be quite lost just yet.

Aston Villa visit Old Trafford on Sunday in the final game before the international break and, if Carrick can follow this with another win, then it will be intriguing to see where the Old Trafford board goes from there.

Carrick may at least have been encouraged by some of the things Bruno Fernandes said after the game, not least that he warranted being dropped against Bournemouth. And it was the captain who kick-started the fightback against Roma, albeit at the second attempt.

He had won the penalty after being fouled by Gianluca Mancini only to then contrive to miss it. But a retake was ordered for encroachment and, given a second bite at the cherry, Fernandes made no mistake.

NO MISTAKE THIS TIME 💪 Bruno Fernandes gets United back in it after a penalty retake 😤 https://t.co/uQdkNs0lXo

When Carlos Baleba pulled up with a hamstring injury within seconds of the restart as he burst into the penalty area, Carrick must have wondered what else could go wrong.

But as United went hell for leather, the home supporters who had spent much of the first half attacking the owners and staging a number of colourful protest acts, suddenly found their voice in a very different way.

From being an atmosphere in which the players clearly felt cowed, Old Trafford was now rallying behind its men in red – and it helped to shake Roma in the process. They had been such good value for their lead, but now they were rocking, and United smelled blood.

There was wave after wave of attack as Roma desperately and often frantically tried to defend their goal, and it took a bad mistake from Leonardo Balerdi, who swung at thin air from Fernandes’s cross and missed the ball, to hand Cunha the chance to equalise.

It was Lacey who speared an inch-perfect pass into Cunha, who turned sharply before drilling a stunning finish in off the near post. Cue bedlam.

Cunha was booked for taking off his shirt as he crowd-surfed bear-chested among the fans and was then sent off minutes later after a poor challenge. A fittingly chaotic end to a crazy night for the match-winner.

The difference to those opening 45 minutes was as stark as it gets. Indeed, the first half felt like a continuation from the fans of their blood-letting against Bournemouth.

When the clock hit 20.05 – a nod to the year 2005 when the Glazers bought the club – a pile of tennis balls were thrown on to the pitch from the Stretford End amid chants of “We Want Glazers Out”. They were quickly followed by cries of “Just like the Glazers, Jim Ratcliffe’s a c---” and “sell the club and f--- off home”.

Jason Wilcox, the club’s director of football, again copped for it. A banner read: “For the love, not the ‘likes’”. When the Champions League music played, hundreds of green and gold balloons – a reference to the club’s original colours and the 2010 protest movement – were released.

On the pitch, United were all over the place. Carrick had dropped Lisandro Martínez after his red card against Chelsea but his replacement Ayden Heaven was at fault for the first goal after getting sucked in and failing to check his shoulder. Had he done, he would have seen Matías Soulé unmarked and in acres of space with Diogo Dalot, United’s left-back, caught high up the pitch. Soulé made no mistake with his finish.

At that point, no one could have reckoned on the comeback that followed. Where it leads, who knows.

Speaking after the match, Michael Carrick was very positive about his side’s performance.

“It was a good night. I have to a lot of credit to the players for starters, showing that character and that quality when we needed it and to the supporters. This place does incredible, magical things,” said Carrick.

“I thought we grew into it the first half  after giving the goals too easily. We spoke at half time about how this place can change, it only takes one moment and it certainly did that and the boys made the most of every opportunity and were fantastic in the end.”

Asked about how he inspired the team at half-time he kept it simple: “Just not to get too disappointed about things. I thought we were coming into the game, getting around their box and it didn’t feel that way to the players because they were carrying too much frustration and disappointment and I knew we were doing some good things in the game against a really good team.

“Playing against man-to-man as much as they are, you probably get more failure than success and it’s still being positive and the boys responded so well to that.”

As for whether this will change United’s momentum now, he was cautious not to get carried away.

“Listen it’s one game. It depends on what happens next and we’ve got to capitalise on that but tonight the boys showed an awful lot,” he said.

“And I thought we came out the second half, unfortunately with Carlos having to go off and Youri coming on the pitch and I thought he was fantastic, he showed everything that he is as a personality, as a character and with his experience to step in the game like that, and the boys just went with the flow and you could feel how positive it was and it was nice to see this place like that again.”

Captain Bruno Fernandes also spoke after the match, acknowledging the difficulties the team has faced.

“It’s tough to say something at the moment to be honest. It’s been a tough period for us, we have not been able to play in the way we want, get the results we want. We’ve done some good bits, but not had the consistency to do it through a whole game to get results and it’s been tough.

“But today was important to get a win. We knew after that we still had the fans with us, we felt we could change it with a goal and something and fortunately we did it today.”

As for his penalty miss and re-take: “First one didn’t go the way I wanted, I did something wrong but I got a second chance and I cleared my head and my mind was only on to get the ball in back of the net.

“It’s been tough for the fans, we understand that. Having that belief from their side helps the team a lot and today was one of those days that Old Trafford came alive.”

After his first start as he returns from injury, Kobbie Mainoo was full of praise for the fans, saying he cherished the relationship the team had with them.

“It’s unlike anything else. We’d do anything for these fans on the pitch, all the love they give us throughout the season it’s only right we repay them and it’s a bit of fun just jumping into the stands with them.”

Speaking to Amazon after the match, Youri Tielemans said: “There has been a lot of pressure on him [Carrick] and that’s how we repay him, with a comeback like this, big character, big fight.”

“We just kept working, we kept believing. We were on the front foot in the second half, we tried to push them into their goal and we succeeded.”

As for whether or not the performance would be enough to keep Carrick in his role at United: “That’s a different question. The only thing we can do is stick behind him, fight for him and fight for the club.

“At the end of the day we are on the pitch and we need to show what we are capable of and tonight, especially in the second half, we showed what we can do and we turned up the gears.

“Let’s hope this is a good turnaround for us and let’s hope we can build on this.”

It’s matchday four of the Champions League and Michael Carrick’s side host their Serie A opponents having failed to win any of their last nine matches across all competitions. Since their win against Sabah back in September (must feel like years ago to Carrick), they have suffered chastening defeats in Europe to Atlético Madrid and then Cesc Fabregas’s Como. All in all, there is the feeling that Carrick is simply a dead man walking, limping towards the international break after the United hierarchy decided on a stay of execution in their crisis talks earlier this month. If the beleaguered manager has any hope at all of hanging on to his job, he needs convincing results tonight and against Aston Villa on the weekend.

Despite the doom-mongering that circles the club, Carrick maintains that he has buried the hatchet with Bruno Fernandes following his captain’s public criticisms of the club, insisting that “the dressing room is a good place” in his pre-match press conference (more on that to come).

The visitors on the other hand, managed by Gian Piero Gasperini – who replaced Claudio Ranieri last summer – are certainly having a better time of it. #1102. Russia is back in world sport, but who is drug testing its athletes?

DW has found that three-quarters of Russia's weightlifting team had no independent out-of-competition testing before this year's world championships, despite the country's doping history.

Fresh questions have emerged over Russia's return to world sport after figures reviewed by DW showed that only four of the 16 Russian weightlifters competing at this year's world championships underwent out-of-competition testing by the International Testing Agency (ITA).

Two-time European champion Anastasiia Romanova, who previously served a two-year doping ban, was among those not tested by the ITA during the first nine months of 2026, according to its quarterly anti-doping reports.

By comparison, all 13 members of the North Korean team underwent at least one ITA test during the same period. North Korea, like Russia, has a history of doping violations in weightlifting.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The ITA, which runs weightlifting's anti-doping program, told DW that it tested all 16 Russian weightlifters "ahead of their participation in the event." DW understands those tests were conducted in Ningbo, China, where the championships are being held.

In a power sport like weightlifting, performance-enhancing drugs are most beneficial during training, when athletes build strength and muscle mass in the months before competition. Some drugs, such as anabolic steroids, may be harder to detect by the time the competition comes around.

Rob Koehler, head of the athlete-led movement Global Athlete, called the lack of out-of-competition testing "absurd."

"Out-of-competition testing is the backbone of anti-doping," Koehler told DW. "Everybody knows there's going to be testing at the event. But not everybody knows when they're going to be tested 365 days a year outside events. It's concerning that the ITA doesn't see this as a red flag."

Marta Nawrocka, the ITA's spokesperson, said that Russian athletes were among the 10 most-tested nationalities in weightlifting this year. She also defended the fact that only two Russian weightlifters feature in the sport's highest-priority testing pool, saying inclusion is based on performance and risk profiles.

"Russia's history of doping in weightlifting remains an important factor in the ITA's risk assessment and testing priorities," Nawrocka said. "Russian weightlifters remain subject to substantial testing activity."

"You simply can't treat Russia like any other country," he said. "It has to have more scrutiny. It has to have more testing. If you don't do that, you're undermining athlete confidence in the system."

The International Weightlifting Federation did not respond to a request for comment.

Weightlifting was one of the sports most implicated in Russia's state-sponsored doping scandal, which came to light after the 2014 Sochi Winter Olympics. It ranked second only to athletics for the number of positive cases identified by Canadian lawyer Richard McLaren in his 2016 report commissioned by WADA, the global anti-doping watchdog.

The scandal led to dozens of Russian athletes being banned across numerous sports. RUSADA, Russia's anti-doping agency, has remained suspended for most of the past decade.

As a result, its Moscow laboratory cannot analyze urine and blood samples, meaning samples collected by the agency must be sent abroad for analysis under what WADA described as a "strict chain of custody."

WADA said it continued to monitor RUSADA but had been unable to gain access to the country to review the agency's suspension because of the "ongoing geopolitical situation."

It added that RUSADA had "collected thousands of samples … including hundreds from weightlifters" so far this year.

"Given the history, WADA remains vigilant when it comes to Russia," James Fitzgerald, WADA's spokesperson, told DW. "We must ensure that no stone is left unturned when it comes to verifying that all the proper testing and other anti-doping activities are taking place."

Despite being suspended, RUSADA still has the power to investigate and prosecute anti-doping cases involving Russian athletes, which critics find difficult to reconcile.

"It's a compounding problem that WADA is still giving them a free pass when it can't even get into Russia to see what they're doing," said Koehler, WADA's former deputy director general.

"There's simply no oversight and no accountability. And quite frankly, I don't think there ever really has been."

Critics also argue that ongoing questions over RUSADA's leadership and independence suggest that little has been fixed in the decade since the McLaren report.

Even the International Olympic Committee (IOC), whose president, Kirsty Coventry, supports the full return of Russian athletes, has acknowledged a "lack of confidence" over RUSADA's governance.

Nawrocka said the IOC had "recently entrusted" the ITA with an expanded role within Russia in the run-up to the Los Angeles Olympics in 2028, but did not explain what the role would involve or when it might begin.

In April, investigative outlet The Insider reported that Veronika Loginova, the agency's head, was in a long-term relationship with an alleged FSB officer. The FSB, Russia's domestic security service, played a central role in covering up positive drug tests at the Sochi Games.

Loginova did not respond to questions for this article but dismissed the allegations at the time as "all this nonsense," writing in an email that she believed "sport exists separate from politics."

WADA confirmed to DW only that its investigations unit was examining the allegations against Loginova and that the inquiry was ongoing.

#1095. Emery endures heaviest European defeat as Villa manager to old foes Barcelona

While there can be little doubt about Unai Emery’s status as an elite manager in the modern game, matches at the Nou Camp continue to be the stuff of nightmares.

His record at Barcelona now reads 15 defeats from 16 matches and this was another difficult evening with Aston Villa unable to banish the demons for the man who has transformed their club.

It was Emery’s 55th birthday and with the Prince of Wales and Prince George both in attendance, Villa fans were hopeful of another memorable European night. But from the moment midfielder João Gomes handed Barcelona their opening goal, it was always going to be an uphill struggle.

Emery has suffered many uncomfortable occasions at this grand old stadium, none more so than the notorious “La Remontada” of 2017 when he last competed here in the Champions League with Paris St-Germain.

This latest visit would become his heaviest defeat in Europe as Villa manager. With three wins from the opening four matches, they still have a fine chance of progressing to the knockout stage. Yet, aside from the mistakes, there will be a sense that Villa could have capitalised more against a team in the midst of a defensive injury crisis. They did have a number of chances in the first half but were left to rue their lack of ruthlessness.

Aston Villa make a mistake at the back and Lamine Yamal makes them pay inside 10 minutes ⚡ 📺 Stream on TNT Sports & HBO Max: https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/1IcWOPMJlt

At the heart of Barcelona’s victory was Lamine Yamal, their outstanding jewel from the academy. The 19-year-old became the highest-scoring teenager in Champions League history, eclipsing the record of 13 he previously shared with Kylian Mbappé, with the opening goal.

Yamal was orchestrating everything from the pace of the match to the volume of the supporters, at one point imploring them to raise the noise in the first half with both arms aloft.

There was also another impressive performance from England international Anthony Gordon and Raphinha, who dedicated his two goals to the memory of Jesus de Miguel, the Tenerife forward, who died on Tuesday.

With that tragedy fresh in the minds and the Nou Camp under construction, it was a peculiar atmosphere at times.

The defeat marked the end of Villa’s 100 per cent record in the competition, with a tough test away at Galatasaray up next before they host PSG in December. They remain high up in the table and have often displayed a propensity to bounce back quickly from defeats.

Emery said: “We are in a process and this was a very good test against a team like Barcelona. We are not at the level we want to achieve but there are a lot of experiences for us to take. Overall, we are competing fantastically in the Champions League and there is still work to do.

“Over the process we’ve had here, we have made mistakes but then overcame them. We accept this defeat but take a lot of information from it.”

Nine years have passed since Emery’s last visit in this competition and time has not proved a great healer.

Then in charge of PSG, Emery witnessed his team surrender a 4-0 first-leg lead to lose 6-5 on aggregate. Any matches where he is involved at the Nou Camp will revive memories of that remarkable comeback. He must have feared a repeat of more pain when Yamal, making his 37th Champions League appearance, rewarded Barcelona’s early pressure.

Villa’s defending needed to be as close to perfect as possible, but they were exposed after a poor error of judgment from Gomes. Under pressure from Barcelona’s attackers, Gomes panicked and played a blind pass into the path of Yamal, who bent his left-footed shot into the corner.

That mistake could have threatened to damage confidence but Villa did respond. Matty Cash’s half-volley from inside the penalty area was only a few inches wide, while Johan Manzambi side-footed wide of the goal after a quick break down the right from Nicolas Jackson.

With Andreas Christensen, Eric García, Xavi Espart and Jules Koundé all absent here, Barcelona’s defence did appear vulnerable. Jackson was targeting the flanks and having his more dangerous moments challenging their high line. Emery paced his technical area, imploring his players to remain focused.

Yet Barcelona’s forward three were always a threat and they increased their lead eight minutes into the second half. Raphinha was given too much room to turn in the penalty area and his shot took a heavy deflection off the heel of Pau Torres to find the bottom corner. Emery was furious, appearing to raise his fist in the air at another poor goal conceded.

“May he rest in peace. In the end, this can happen to anyone. The truth is that it’s very tough. When we saw the news this morning, it was complicated. I’m incredibly shocked and sad. Unai Emery has managed more than 1,100 matches but will never forget the drama of “La Remontada” as he returns to the scene on Tuesday night.

Emery is back at the Nou Camp in the Champions League for the first time since one of the most epic games in the history of the competition. While in charge of Paris St-Germain nine years ago, Emery took his team to Barcelona with a 4-0 lead from the round-of-16 first leg. Yet he was left stunned as Barcelona recovered to win the rematch 6-1, with three goals in the final seven minutes and the winner proving hugely controversial.

No such luck, however, and it is pretty torrential at the moment. Football updates to follow.

Aston Villa have made the trip over to Spain to take on Barcelona in the Champions League on matchday four. These teams last met all the way back in 1983, when they met in the European Super Cup. Barcelona won the first leg 1-0 at home before Aston Villa claimed a 3-0 victory at Villa Park, meaning Villa progressed 3-1 on aggregate.

Aston Villa have made the perfect start to their Champions League campaign, winning all three games, beating Club Brugge, Fenerbahce and Viking, scoring 12 goals in the process. Unai Emery’s side drew 1-1 at home against Fulham in the league on Saturday. Emery, who celebrates his 55th birthday today, has a very dismal record against Barcelona, taking just three wins from 30 matches. His last Champions League game at the Nou Camp was infamous as his PSG side lost 6-1 to go out in the last 16 back in 2017 despite winning the first leg of that tie 4-0.

“In 1982, Villa won the European Cup, and we like to think about playing in this competition again and trying to repeat that success,” Emery said. “Barcelona are favourites for what they have done in the last ten years; now they need to prove why they are favourites.

“[Barcelona] have [Lamine] Yamal. He is a special player. You can see in him as a player who could end up being the best. He needs a few things but he could end up being a great player. Rodri gives personality to the team. They have [Anthony] Gordon giving them speed and hard work. They have Pedri or Fermin [Lopez] as offensive midfielders.”

Barcelona started strongly in the Champions League, winning their first two games, but lost 4-2 at defending champions PSG last time out. They warmed up for this match with an emphatic 6-1 win over Alaves in La Liga on Saturday. That victory gives them a two-point lead at the summit of La Liga.

“We know that at this level, anything can happen,” Barcelona boss Hansi Flick said. “Against Real Madrid, the result could have been different. These are special matches, but we are staying confident. It is normal to focus more on our last two defeats, but I have confidence in my team, which showed it again on Saturday. Now, we are focused on the Champions League, with the goal of finishing in the top eight. For me, he [Unai Emery] is one of the best coaches in the world and he has reaped extraordinary successes. His team’s style of play is clear and very well organised. Just look at how they execute set pieces; it is something impressive. Their confidence in themselves is unmatched. It will be a tough match against a great team and a great coach.”

#1094. RANGERS 3 ABERDEEN 2: Amid all the thrills and spills, McInnes' triple switch sparks second-half revival

By JOHN MCGARRY, SCOTTISH CHIEF SPORTS FEATURE WRITER

Published: 18:40 EST, 24 November 2026 | Updated: 18:50 EST, 24 November 2026

When these sides last met in the league at the end of August, Rangers were in such a dark place that you wondered if their season was already destined to be another thoroughly miserable episode.

Coming just three days after going out of Europe — for the second time — to an ordinary Jablonec team, the slender win Derek McInnes’ side claimed at Pittodrie that day felt like a can being kicked down the road.

In those early weeks, the players looked lost. The manager admitted that he didn’t know what style of football he was watching. The supporters were preparing for a long, hard winter.

It’s remarkable what can come from one scruffy win on the road. From that point to this, McInnes’ men have now gone 14 games unbeaten in all competitions.

They have the League Cup final to look forward to next month. They are now just one point behind Celtic in the Premiership and look eminently capable of putting in a serious challenge for the title. In keeping with so many performances throughout this run, however, this wasn’t particularly convincing. Flat and rudderless for 45 minutes, Rangers were deservedly a goal behind at the interval.

Credit where it’s due, though. Their response at the outset of the second period was outstanding with three goals coming in 11 minutes courtesy of Ryan Naderi, Djeidi Gassama and Nico Raskin.

That ought to have been the platform for many more to follow. But the performance slipped back a level. Aberdeen scored once and could easily have scored again.

Raskin (right) and Gassama celebrate after combining to put Rangers 3-1 up

Naderi capitalises on Muller's mishandling to fire Rangers level at the start of the second half

It was a truly thrilling match, full of slip-ups, incidents and moments of brilliance. The final stages were a tough watch for the home fans who hoped against hope that they’d see their side ease towards a routine victory.

As at Fir Park on Saturday, though, Rangers found a way and added another win to the ledger. And provided that remains the case in the coming weeks and months, none of the light blue legions will be complaining.

Despite ultimately not having quite enough to take something, Aberdeen manager Mario Frick will have been encouraged by much of what he saw here.

Had it not been for that atrocious spell at the outset of the second period, he’d have fancied his men to take something.

They certainly fashioned plenty of opportunities. It was the defensive side of the game which ultimately cost them.

McInnes drafted in Kevin Kelsy, James Penrice and Ben Godfrey with Dujon Sterling, Tuur Rommens and Kim Minsu dropping out. There was a change of shape too, with a switch to a 3-5-2. For the longest time, it did not work.

Lyons gets his head to Marshall's corner to put Aberdeen in front in the first half

While Frick kept faith with the diamond-shaped midfield which served him so well in Ayrshire, he made three changes. In came Ayoub Mouloua, Afeez Aremu and Findlay Marshall at the expense of Hicham Mahou, Ante Palaversa and Stuart Armstrong.

Before the game, there was a minute’s silence in memory of the late, great Ralph Brand. What a pity a couple of clowns in the visiting section were unable to keep their mouths shut for that long.

Rangers started brightly with Penrice’s delivery from the left causing chaos. Dan Neil had a stab at it, then Naderi. Aberdeen survived.

Once Frick’s side settled, Nicky Devlin’s cross was met by Marshall. His header was straight at Ivor Pandur.

Rangers’ general play was broken, their build-up more ponderous than patient. Gassama did manage to drop a shoulder and get a strike away but Aremu’s positioning ensured Marius Muller was untroubled.

Naderi was again Rangers’ most effective player, although the bar was set pretty low initially. The Czech’s lay-off invited Godfrey to let fly. His strike was well off target.

While Gassama got into plenty of promising positions, his crossing continually let him down early on. On the other flank, Badredine Bouanani could not do right for doing wrong.

When the ball broke kindly to Naderi on the edge of the box, Ibrox expected the net to bulge. This time the man of the moment fired over. Rangers’ efforts in the first half were summed up by Naderi being tripped by Gavin Molloy on the edge of the box. Bouanani’s effort from the free-kick was woeful.

Aberdeen were aggressive and organised. And when the moment arose, they went forward in numbers.

McInnes shows his delight after his half-time changes helped turn the game around

They edged in front on the half hour after Marshall won a corner which was a consequence of Frick’s men being prepared to back themselves.

Marshall curled the set-piece deep to the far post. Brad Lyons seemed to be invisible to those in light blue as he made a late run. Olwethu Makhanya belatedly reacted but it was too late.

Lyons got enough on his header to beat Pandur and force Raskin to make the block behind his keeper.

The minute the scoreboard indicated that VAR were checking for a goal, you suspected the Belgian hadn’t done quite enough to keep it out. After a lengthy delay came confirmation of that fact.

How would Rangers respond up until the break? Not terribly well. Lyons’ crude foul on Gassama gave Bouanani a chance to make amends with a set-piece. This one smashed into the wall. Seconds later, the winger fired well over the top when he ought to have done better.

The Dons could easily have doubled their advantage. Jack Milne carried well and rattled the ball into Kevin Nisbet’s feet. The forward played a smart pass around the corner. Mouloua was only denied by a terrific save from Pandur.

There was still time for Mouloua to be thwarted by the outstretched leg of Makhanya as he moved to turn home a cut back.

Bluntly, it was no surprise that McInnes made three changes at the break. Off came Godfrey, Kelsy and Bouanani. On went Minsu, Rommens and Findlay Curtis. The impact was extraordinary.

Re-energised, within 45 seconds Rangers were level. Minsu’s speculative shot did come through heavy traffic. Still, Muller had to hold it. Credit to Naderi for anticipating the fumble. The instant it bounced towards him, he instinctively lashed it home for his 10th of the season. Subdued to that point, the home fans roared their approval. And they’d quickly be off their seats again.

As Aberdeen’s attack broke down, Naderi played a simple pass into space. Gassama had too much pace for the chasing pack. Did he have the finishing? Absolutely. What a turnaround.

Gassama squeezes his shot under Muller to put the home side ahead just after the restart

Two goals in 90 seconds then became three in 11 second-half minutes. Gassama did superbly to motor down the left, look up and play in Raskin. The Belgian smashed the ball back across goal and in.

That should have been that. Yet three minutes later, the Dons were back within a goal of McInnes’ men. Afforded too much time on the left, Alexander Briedl picked out Marshall with his cross. Marshall swept it home with his left foot via the inside of the post.

Remarkably, the Dons might well have levelled. Pandur made a fine save when Minsu threatened to turn an Aberdeen corner into his own net. The ball bounced off Nisbet and just wide.

Terrific throughout, Marshall saw a good strike whistle just wide. The fact the Dons made Rangers sweat for the win will be some consolation.

#1090. Exercise coaching boosts colon cancer survival

Evidence suggests exercise can keep more cancer patients alive. But what does "living longer" actually mean, and who does it apply to?

In 2025, an international trial found that people treated for colon cancer were more likely to be alive eight years later if they had received long-term exercise coaching.

The question facing doctors now is less whether people with cancer should exercise, and rather how they should build it into routine care.   In the US, that shift is reaching hospital standards. From January 2027, breast cancer centers must screen patients' physical function and recommend exercise or physical therapy where needed.

Yet experts caution that the trial's findings may not apply to every cancer or every patient.

The 2025 trial, called CHALLENGE, was led by the Canadian Cancer Trials Group. It began enrolling patients in 2009 and published its results in 2025.

The trial's 889 participants came from six countries, most from Canada and Australia. All had finished surgery and chemotherapy for stage 2 or 3 colon cancer, which had not spread to distant organs.

Half received only health education materials on exercise and healthy eating. The other half additionally met a physical activity consultant for three years.

In the exercise group, the target was similar to adding 45 to 60 minutes of brisk walking, three to four times a week. The amount and type of activity varied from person to person, said Tormod Skogstad Nilsen, a cancer exercise researcher in Norway. But he said participants achieved lasting increases in their physical activity.

Exercise helped. People in the exercise group were less likely to see their cancer come back, to develop a new cancer or to die. In all, 93 had at least one of these setbacks, compared with 131 in the health education group.

In cancer research, living longer usually means a larger share of people is still alive at a given point. It does not promise anyone a set number of extra years.

Eight years after joining CHALLENGE, about 90 of every 100 people in the exercise group were alive, compared with about 83 of every 100 in the health education group. That is about 7% more people alive in the group who had guided exercise.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

For people without cancer, the evidence comes from studies that follow people's habits and health over many years. These can show a link, but not prove cause and effect. Active people may also eat better or smoke less.

In another 2025 study, more than 85,000 adults in the United Kingdom wore a wrist tracker for a week. Over about six years, those who moved most had a 26% lower risk of 13 cancers, including breast and colorectal cancer, than those who moved least.

Even light activity, such as household chores, was linked to lower risk. The link held after researchers accounted for lifestyle, weight and other health conditions.

Earlier research, based on people's self-reporting, has led to similar conclusions. A 2016 analysis of 1.44 million adults in the US and Europe linked free-time activity to a lower risk of many cancers, largely regardless of weight or smoking.

A trial to prove prevention is unlikely: Many cancers take years to develop, so it would need huge numbers of people followed for a long time.

CHALLENGE included only people with colon cancer. But how it picked participants offers a clue: Before joining, they had to pass a fitness test.

Anna Campbell, a professor of clinical exercise science at Edinburgh Napier University in Scotland, sees that as a guide.

"I think patients with any other cancer stage II and III who have a reasonable baseline level of fitness and no major comorbidities that would prevent them from undertaking moderate to vigorous activity could be considered for similar interventions," she said. Comorbidities are other health conditions.

Nilsen noted some people decline to join exercise trials because they feel too unwell or tired, or do not want to exercise. "Hence, study populations are typically younger, 'healthier', and most times slightly more motivated compared to a clinical population," he said.

The coaching aimed to make activity a lasting habit, and Campbell said that is where the trial's value lies.

"The main success of the study is that it enabled the participants to become independent exercisers staying active in a safe and effective and individualized way," she said.

Nilsen agreed. Helping people become more active "in their own environment," without depending on a well-equipped training center, "would likely lead to more sustainable activity behavioral changes," he said.

He is wary of fixed targets, however. "Exercise should be tailored to each individual and the challenges they face, rather than striving to reach a given minimum of exercise required," though health care resources may not always allow it, he added.

In a 2024 survey of 549 people with cancer, only one in 10 had been referred to an exercise service. Yet almost three in four thought their oncologist should raise the subject.

"There are some excellent examples of effective pathways but these are few and far between," said Campbell. Good services bring everyone on board, from surgeons to community fitness instructors.

"Ideally, one person in the clinical setting needs to champion the program to link all the team together."

Campbell expects CHALLENGE's regular coaching will be cut back in everyday care. Apps and live online group sessions could still work, she said, if run by properly trained staff.

One recent study of live online exercise engaged patients from poorer backgrounds, in rural areas and with advanced cancer. "It answered some of the barriers, such as cost, travel and lack of confidence," she said.

Patients can ask their care team what exercise is safe for them and what support exists.

According to Nilsen, a training session can bring structure and company. "You made it here, despite your feeling unwell or fatigued this morning, so you feel mastery based on that," he said.
